page_content:
Temple: Birla Mandir Hyderabad
Temple ID: T0009
Section: overview

overview: Birla Mandir is one of the most prominent Hindu temples in Hyderabad, Telangana. Dedicated to Lord Sri Venkateswara (Balaji), the temple stands atop Naubat Pahad, overlooking the city and Hussain Sagar Lake. Constructed entirely of white Rajasthan marble (about 2,000 tons), it is renowned for its peaceful atmosphere, architectural beauty, and panoramic views of Hyderabad. Built by the Birla Foundation (1970–1976) under the guidance of Swami Ranganathananda of the Ramakrishna Mission, it blends Dravidian, Rajasthani, and Utkala architectural styles. Every year, thousands of devotees and tourists visit to seek blessings and admire its magnificent craftsmanship.
summary: Birla Mandir, atop Naubat Pahad in Khairatabad, Hyderabad, is a prominent Vaishnavite temple dedicated to Lord Sri Venkateswara (Balaji). Built entirely of pure white Rajasthan marble by the Birla Foundation between 1970 and 1976 under Swami Ranganathananda of the Ramakrishna Mission, it harmoniously blends Dravidian, Rajasthani and Utkala architecture, with intricate carvings from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavad Gita. The sanctum houses an ~11-foot granite idol of Lord Venkateswara, with additional shrines to Padmavati, Andal, Shiva, Lakshmi, Ganesha, Hanuman and Sai Baba. It is a major centre of Vaishnavite worship and a popular tourist landmark overlooking Hussain Sagar.

history.section: Construction
history.content: Birla Mandir was built by the Birla Foundation under the guidance of Swami Ranganathananda of the Ramakrishna Mission. Construction began in 1970 and was completed in 1976. Approximately 2,000 tons of pure white marble from Rajasthan were used. The temple was established to provide devotees with a serene place of worship in the heart of Hyderabad while promoting India's rich cultural and spiritual heritage.

sthala_puranam: Built with 2,000 tons of white marble, blending Dravidian, Rajasthani, and Odia styles. The idol of Lord Venkateswara is 11 ft tall under a lotus canopy. The hill 'Naubath Pahad' was historically used by Mughals/Nizams for drum proclamations.

architecture: The temple is built entirely from white marble and showcases a harmonious blend of Dravidian (South Indian), Rajasthani (North Indian), and Utkala (Odisha) architectural styles. The sanctum houses a magnificent granite idol of Lord Venkateswara, standing about 11 feet tall. Intricate carvings depicting scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Bhagavad Gita adorn the temple walls and pillars. The elevated Naubat Pahad location offers breathtaking views of Hussain Sagar Lake, Tank Bund, and the Hyderabad city skyline.

Best time to visit is early morning or evening for the best light and fewer crowds.'

page_content:
Temple: Swarnagiri Sri Venkateswara Swamy Devasthanam
Temple ID: T0023
Section: overview

overview: Swarnagiri Sri Venkateswara Swamy Devasthanam, also known as Yadadri Tirumala Devasthanam, is a modern Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Venkateswara Swamy, located atop the scenic Manepally Hills (Swarnagiri Hills) in Anantharam Rural, Bhuvanagiri, Yadadri-Bhuvanagiri District, Telangana — about 47 km from Hyderabad. Built by the Manepally family (Manepally Charitable Trust / Srivari Seva Trust) on 22 acres of their own land, construction began in 2018 and the temple was consecrated on 6 March 2024 by Tridandi Chinna Jeeyar Swamy, following Sri Pancharatra Agama and Tennacharya Sampradaya. The temple features a 12-foot black-granite Venkateswara idol (the largest in Telangana), a 40-foot monolithic Hanuman, a 27-foot Anjaneya, a five-storied Vimana Gopuram, four Rajagopurams, a 1.5-ton bronze bell (India's second-largest), a water-filled Jala Narayana Swamy Sannidhi, multiple sub-shrines (Padmavati, Lakshmi Narasimha, Bhu Varaha, Madan Gopal Krishna, Anjaneya, Ganesha, Vakula Matha, Garuda, Ramanujacharya, Godadevi), and 108 steps leading up to the hilltop. Daily footfall is 70,000–80,000 (crossing 1 lakh on festivals). General darshan is free; special darshan tickets start at ₹50. Open 5 AM to 9 PM daily.

history.section: Founder's Family Story & Motivation
history.content: The idea of building Swarnagiri Temple came from a deeply personal miracle in the Manepally family. In 2016, Vijayalaxmi, the wife of Sri Manepally Rama Rao, had a life-threatening accident in an escalator that broke her bones and pushed her into a coma. The doctors gave up. It was the holy water (tirtham) that somebody brought from Tirupati that brought her back to life. The Manepally family, in thanksgiving, decided to use their own land to build a temple to Lord Venkateswara — to celebrate the miracle and offer a Tirupati-like spiritual hub closer to Hyderabad. The Manepally family is a prominent jewellery business family from Telangana, led by Sri Manepally Rama Rao (a businessman and philanthropist) along with his two sons, trustees Smt Manepally Vijaya Lakshmi, Manepally Murali Krishna, Manepally Sri Latha, Manepally Gopi Krishna, and Manepally Mamatha. Under the Manepally Charitable Trust (also called the Srivari Seva Trust, established 30 January 2024), the family dedicated approximately 22 acres of prime land on a hillock that overlooks the historic Bhongir landscape. The name 'Swarnagiri' (meaning 'Golden Hill') was chosen to reflect the inner radiance and spiritual wealth the temple aims to bestow.

sthala_puranam: Swarnagiri Temple does not have a traditional ancient Sthala Puranam because it is a modern temple — built between 2018 and 2024 and consecrated only in 2024. The site's sacred character is derived from: (1) The Manepally family's personal miracle in 2016 (recovery of Smt Manepally Vijaya Lakshmi from a coma after tirtham from Tirupati), which inspired the temple construction; (2) The temple's dedication to Lord Venkateswara Swamy, whose main idol is a 12-foot black-granite statue (the largest Venkateswara idol in Telangana); (3) The Prana Pratishtha and Kumbhabhishekam performed by Tridandi Chinna Jeeyar Swamy in March 2024 — which infuses the hilltop with divine energy and authentic Sri Vaishnava Agama sanctity; (4) The 108 steps symbolising the spiritual climb to the sanctum; (5) The 1.5-ton bronze bell (India's second largest temple bell); and (6) The hilltop location (Manepally / Swarnagiri Hills) overlooking the historic Bhongir landscape — chosen for its picturesque setting that enhances the spiritual experience.

religious_significance: Swarnagiri is significant in five ways: (1) It houses the largest Venkateswara idol in Telangana (12 feet tall, in black granite, gold- and silver-adorned); (2) It is consecrated by Tridandi Chinna Jeeyar Swamy — one of the most revered Sri Vaishnava Acharyas — so every ritual follows authentic Pancharatra Agama and Tennacharya Sampradaya; (3) It is widely considered a 'Tirupati of Telangana' — offering Tirumala-like darshan within 50 km of Hyderabad for devotees who cannot travel to Andhra Pradesh frequently; (4) It draws 70,000–80,000 devotees daily (crossing 1 lakh on festivals) and is rapidly becoming one of the most-visited pilgrimage sites in Telangana; (5) It is part of the larger Yadadri temple circuit, along with Yadadri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple and Bhongir Fort.

spiritual_significance: Devotees believe that praying to Lord Venkateswara at Swarnagiri brings financial stability, career success, and fulfilment of wishes. The 12-foot black-granite idol is considered especially powerful because of the Agama Shastra rituals performed at consecration and the daily pancha-samskara rituals. The illuminated Jala Narayana Swamy Sannidhi (water-filled sanctum) is a unique feature that gives visitors a meditative experience in the evening. The 40-foot monolithic Hanuman is venerated for protection, courage, and removal of obstacles. The 108 steps symbolise the spiritual ascent to the divine. The 1.5-ton bronze bell is rung during aarti and is said to carry prayers to the divine. Many devotees also visit Swarnagiri as part of the Yadadri temple circuit (Yadadri + Swarnagiri + Bhongir Fort + Kolanupaka Jain Temple) for a half-day spiritual trip from Hyderabad.

darshan_and_tickets.general_darshan: Free for all devotees. Timings: 5:00 AM – 9:00 PM daily (with break 12:30 PM – 1:30 PM). Free Mahaprasad is distributed from 1:30 PM – 2:30 PM (per hyderabadtourism.travel).
darshan_and_tickets.special_darshan: Seegra Darshanam: ₹50 per person; Srivari Donor Darshan: ₹300 per person; Seva Darshan: ₹500 per person. Online booking available via swarnagiritemple.com / ytdtemple.com / tickets99.com.
darshan_and_tickets.ticket_details: Free general darshan. Seegra Darshanam ₹50. Srivari Donor Darshan ₹300. Special sevas range from ₹100 (Archana) to ₹51,000 (Vishesha Kalyanam). Poolangi Seva (Tue/Thu/Sat): ₹21,000. Srivari Nitya Kalyanam: ₹2,001. Sahasra Nama Archana: ₹1,100. Vedha Ashirvachanam: ₹2,501. Tickets can be booked online at swarnagiritemple.com, ytdtemple.com, or via tickets99.com. Prasadam items (Laddu, Vada, Pulihora, Tulabaram items) can be purchased online. Photography is restricted inside the temple premises.

dress_code: Swarnagiri Temple follows a simple and traditional dress code that aligns with Vaishnava temple customs. Men: dhoti-kurta, pancha or formal pants paired with a shirt are appropriate. Women: saree, salwar kameez, churidar, or long skirt with dupatta. Traditional attire is especially recommended during special sevas or festive occasions. Maintain proper dress and decorum to preserve the sanctity of the temple. Avoid shorts, sleeveless tops, mini skirts, ripped jeans, or any revealing outfits inside the temple premises.

accommodation.availability: On-site temple accommodation is available at Swarnagiri Sree Venkateswara Swami Devasthanam — including AC rooms with 2, 4, and 6 beds, a 2 BHK cottage, and a Dormitory Hall (per yatradham.org). Meals and parking facilities are available for all guests. Off-site options are also available in Bhuvanagiri town (~10 km), Bhongir, Yadadri, and Hyderabad.
accommodation.booking_process: Book accommodation via yatradham.org (online) or via the temple's official website. Off-site hotels can be booked via standard hotel platforms.
accommodation.first_come_basis: On-site temple rooms may be partly available on a first-come basis; advance booking is recommended especially during weekends and festivals.
accommodation.price_range: On-site temple accommodation starts at ₹789/night (per yatradham.org). AC rooms and 2 BHK cottage would be more expensive. Off-site: Bhuvanagiri/Bhongir/Yadadri budget ₹800–₹1,500/night; Hyderabad full range from ₹1,000 to ₹10,000+/night.

travel.road: Located on the Manepally Hills near Bhuvanagiri, ~47 km from Hyderabad (1.5–2 hours drive). Take NH 163 (Uppal → Ghatkesar → Bhongir → Swarnagiri) or the ORR Warangal NH 163 via the Ghatkesar exit. TGSRTC operates special buses from MGBS (Mahatma Gandhi Bus Stand) and JBS (Jubilee Bus Stand) to Yadadri, with onward connection to Swarnagiri. Buses from Hyderabad MGBS to Yadadri: 57 km; from JBS to Yadadri: 55.8 km (per official bus table). Private buses also run.
travel.rail: Nearest railway station is Bhongir (Bhuvanagiri) Railway Station — ~10 km. Yadadri Railway Station — ~18 km. travel_tips: Visit during early morning (5:00–8:00 AM) or evening (4:00–8:00 PM) for a peaceful darshan and to see the illuminated Jala Narayana Swamy Sannidhi.
travel_tips: Carry minimal belongings for quicker security checks; cameras and mobile phones are not allowed inside the temple.
travel_tips: Maintain silence and discipline during darshan.
travel_tips: Wear traditional attire (dhoti/saree/churidar) per temple guidelines.
travel_tips: Online ticket booking is available via swarnagiritemple.com / ytdtemple.com / tickets99.com.
travel_tips: Combine your visit with Yadadri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple (~18 km), Bhongir Fort (~10 km), Surendrapuri (~20 km), and Kolanupaka Jain Temple (~35 km) for a full-day pilgrimage circuit.
travel_tips: Free Mahaprasad is distributed from 1:30 PM – 2:30 PM — plan to be present then if you want to partake.
travel_tips: TGSRTC runs special buses from MGBS and JBS to Yadadri (with onward connection to Swarnagiri).
travel_tips: If driving, take NH 163 (Uppal → Ghatkesar → Bhongir → Swarnagiri) or the ORR Warangal NH 163 via the Ghatkesar exit.
travel_tips: Avoid visiting during peak festival days (Brahmotsavam) if you want to avoid huge crowds; daily footfall is already 70,000–80,000.

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: What is Swarnagiri Sri Venkateswara Swamy Devasthanam?
faq.answer: Swarnagiri is a modern Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Venkateswara Swamy, located atop the scenic Manepally Hills in Anantharam Rural, Bhuvanagiri, Yadadri-Bhuvanagiri District, Telangana — about 47 km from Hyderabad. Built by the Manepally family (Manepally Charitable Trust / Srivari Seva Trust) on 22 acres of their own land, it was consecrated on 6 March 2024 by Tridandi Chinna Jeeyar Swamy, following Sri Pancharatra Agama and Tennacharya Sampradaya. The temple features a 12-foot black-granite Venkateswara idol (the largest in Telangana), a 40-foot monolithic Hanuman, a five-storied Vimana Gopuram, four Rajagopurams, a 1.5-ton bronze bell (India's second-largest), and a water-filled Jala Narayana Swamy Sannidhi.

page_content:
Temple: Swarnagiri Sri Venkateswara Swamy Devasthanam
Temple ID: T0023
Section: faq

faq.answer: Swarnagiri was built by the Manepally family, led by Sri Manepally Rama Rao (a prominent businessman and philanthropist) along with his two sons, trustees Smt Manepally Vijaya Lakshmi, Manepally Murali Krishna, Manepally Sri Latha, Manepally Gopi Krishna, and Manepally Mamatha. The temple was constructed under the Manepally Charitable Trust (also called the Srivari Seva Trust, established 30 January 2024). The idea of building the temple came from a deeply personal miracle in 2016, when Smt Manepally Vijaya Lakshmi recovered from a life-threatening escalator accident and coma after tirtham (holy water) from Tirupati was brought to her. The family, in thanksgiving, decided to use their own land to build a temple to Lord Venkateswara. Construction began in 2018, and the temple was consecrated on 6 March 2024 by Tridandi Chinna Jeeyar Swamy.

page_content:
Temple: Swarnagiri Sri Venkateswara Swamy Devasthanam
Temple ID: T0023
Section: faq

faq.answer: Swarnagiri is a modern masterpiece of Dravidian architecture, drawing inspiration from the Pallava, Chola, Chalukya, and Vijayanagara styles. The temple complex is spread across 22 acres atop the Manepally Hills. Key architectural features include: (1) Four majestic Rajagopurams (temple gateways) on four sides of the prakara; (2) A five-storied Vimana Gopuram rising above the Garbha Griha; (3) The Garbha Griha houses a 12-foot black-granite idol of Lord Venkateswara (the largest in Telangana), flanked by Sridevi and Bhu Devi; (4) A 40-foot monolithic Hanuman statue; (5) A 1.5-ton bronze bell (India's second-largest); (6) A water-filled Jala Narayana Swamy Sannidhi (illuminated visual highlight in evenings); (7) Sub-shrines of Padmavati, Lakshmi Narasimha, Bhu Varaha, Madan Gopal Krishna, Anjaneya, Ganesha, Vakula Matha, Garuda, Ramanujacharya, Godadevi; (8) 108 steps leading up to the temple complex; (9) A 40-foot Ratham (chariot); and (10) A Pushkarini (sacred tank) with Vedic scholars' (Veda Murthis) idols.

faq.answer: The most important festival is Brahmotsavam — a 10-day grand celebration held annually between March and April (similar to the Tirumala Brahmotsavam). Other major festivals include Vaikunta Ekadashi (Dec/Jan), Rathasapthami, Sri Rama Navami, Sri Krishna Janmashtami, Hanuman Jayanti (March/April), Deepavali, and Vinayaka Chavithi (Ganesh Chaturthi) with Navaratri celebrations. During festivals, darshan timings are extended, special sevas are performed, and footfall exceeds 1 lakh.
faq.id: FAQ007
faq.question: How much time do I need at Swarnagiri?
faq.answer: Plan to spend at least half a day to fully explore Swarnagiri. The temple has a sprawling 22-acre complex with multiple sub-shrines. Most visitors combine Swarnagiri with Yadadri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple (~15–18 km), Bhongir Fort (~10 km), Surendrapuri (~20 km), and Kolanupaka Jain Temple (~35 km) for a full-day pilgrimage circuit from Hyderabad.

faq.question: How do I reach Swarnagiri Temple from Hyderabad?
faq.answer: By road: ~47 km from Hyderabad (1.5–2 hours drive). Take NH 163 (Uppal → Ghatkesar → Bhongir → Swarnagiri) or the ORR Warangal NH 163 via the Ghatkesar exit. By bus: TGSRTC operates special buses from MGBS (Mahatma Gandhi Bus Stand) and JBS (Jubilee Bus Stand) to Yadadri (57 km and 55.8 km respectively), with onward connection to Swarnagiri. By train: nearest railway station is Bhongir (~10 km) or Yadadri (~18 km). Direct trains from Secunderabad to Yadadri: Krishna Express (17406), SC-WL (746), SC BDCR EXP (17659), HYB KZJ SPL (7758). By air: nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~50–71 km).

faq.answer: Swarnagiri Temple follows a simple and traditional dress code that aligns with Vaishnava temple customs. For men: dhoti-kurta, pancha, or formal pants paired with a shirt are appropriate. For women: saree, salwar kameez, churidar, or long skirt with dupatta. Traditional attire is especially recommended during special sevas or festive occasions. Avoid shorts, sleeveless tops, mini skirts, ripped jeans, or any revealing outfits inside the temple premises. Maintain proper dress and decorum to preserve the sanctity of the temple.
faq.id: FAQ012
faq.question: Is Swarnagiri Temple accessible for elderly and disabled visitors?
faq.answer: Yes — Swarnagiri is wheelchair-accessible at the entrance and exit (per JustDial). Lifts are available for senior citizens and those unable to climb the 108 steps (per bloggymaster.com). Free Mahaprasad is distributed from 1:30 PM – 2:30 PM daily. There is ample parking at the foot of the hill. Photography is restricted inside the temple (cameras and mobile phones not allowed). Switch off your mobile phones at the temples; don't carry weapons or head gear (helmets, caps, turbans) inside the temple premises. Smoking and alcohol consumption are prohibited.

Swarnagiri Sri Venkateswara Swamy Devasthanam
best_time_to_visit: October to March is the most pleasant weather window. Special days: Brahmotsavam (10 days in March/April — the most important festival), Vaikunta Ekadashi (Dec/Jan), Hanuman Jayanti (March/April), Sri Rama Navami, Sri Krishna Janmashtami. For the most comfortable experience, visit on a weekday morning (5:00–8:00 AM) or in the evening (4:00–8:00 PM). The illuminated Jala Narayana Swamy Sannidhi is best viewed in the evening. Most visitors combine Swarnagiri with Yadadri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple (~18 km), Bhongir Fort (~10 km), Surendrapuri (~20 km), and Kolanupaka Jain Temple (~35 km) for a full-day pilgrimage circuit from Hyderabad.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Jogulamba Devi Temple
Temple ID: T0006
Section: overview

overview: Sri Jogulamba Devi Temple, popularly known as Jogulamba Temple, is one of the most sacred Shakti temples in India. Located at Alampur in Jogulamba Gadwal district of Telangana, near the confluence of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers, it is revered as one of the 18 Maha Shakti Peethas and the Western Gateway (Paschima Dwaram) of the Srisailam Temple. The name 'Jogulamba' comes from the Telugu 'Yogula Amma' meaning 'Mother of Yogis'. The Goddess is worshipped in her fierce Ugra form for protection, courage, prosperity, and spiritual enlightenment. The temple stands adjacent to the 7th-century Bala Brahmeswara Swamy Temple and the Navabrahma Temples of the Badami Chalukya dynasty.
summary: Sri Jogulamba Devi Temple at Alampur, Telangana, is one of the 18 Maha Shakti Peethas — where, per tradition, the upper teeth of Goddess Sati fell. Dedicated to Goddess Jogulamba (a fierce form of Parvati), it lies near the confluence of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers and serves as the Western Gateway (Paschima Dwaram) of Srisailam Temple. The original 7th-century Badami Chalukya temple was destroyed in the 14th century by Bahmani invaders; the idol was safeguarded in the Bala Brahmeswara Temple for centuries and was ceremoniously reinstalled at the reconstructed temple in 2005. Today it is one of the most visited Shakti Peethas in South India, especially during Sharannavaratri.

history.section: Origin (7th Century CE)
history.content: The temple has a rich history dating back to the 7th century CE. The original temple was built during the rule of the Badami Chalukyas, who also constructed the famous Navabrahma temples at Alampur. Jogulamba Devi was worshipped alongside Lord Bala Brahmeswara, making Alampur an important centre for both Shakti and Shaiva traditions.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Jogulamba Devi Temple
Temple ID: T0006
Section: history

history.content: During the 14th century, the temple suffered destruction during invasions by the Bahmani rulers. To protect the sacred idol, devotees shifted the original idol of Goddess Jogulamba (along with her two shaktis Chandi and Mundi) to the nearby Bala Brahmeswara Swamy Temple, where it remained safely worshipped for several centuries. The original temple lay in ruins until the early 21st century, when a new temple was constructed at the original site and the idol was ceremoniously reinstalled in 2005. The original Chandi and Mundi idols remain in the Bala Brahmeswara Swamy Temple; new idols were placed in the new Jogulamba Temple.

history.legends: The original idol was hidden in the Bala Brahmeswara Swamy Temple for ~6 centuries to protect it from 14th-century Bahmani invaders.

religious_significance: Jogulamba Temple is one of the 18 Maha Shakti Peethas (where the upper teeth of Goddess Sati are believed to have fallen) and the Western Gateway (Paschima Dwaram) of the Srisailam Temple. Worshipping Goddess Jogulamba and the adjacent Lord Bala Brahmeswara together is believed to bring the combined blessings of Shakti and Shiva, ensuring complete spiritual fulfillment.
spiritual_significance: Devotees believe worship here removes negative energies, grants protection from evil forces, and blesses them with courage, prosperity and spiritual strength. The Goddess in her Ugra Roopa symbolises the destruction of evil and the protection of devotees, yet is considered a compassionate mother to sincere worshippers. The temple is especially popular among devotees practising Shakti Upasana, and is sought for relief from obstacles, family problems, health issues and planetary afflictions.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Jogulamba Devi Temple
Temple ID: T0006
Section: architecture

architecture: The temple is a beautiful blend of traditional South Indian temple architecture and modern design. Reconstructed in 2005 at its original location in the Chalukyan style to complement the nearby ancient Navabrahma Temples, the complex features a magnificent entrance, spacious mandapams, and beautifully carved pillars. The sanctum houses the fierce idol of Goddess Jogulamba in her Ugra Roopa — seated on a corpse with disheveled hair, a protruding tongue, and a scorpion, frog and lizard adorning her hair. A water pool surrounds the temple, creating a cool atmosphere. Adjacent are the ancient Bala Brahmeswara Swamy Temple and the Navabrahma Temples. The premises are clean, well-maintained and surrounded by gardens. Ashta Dasha Shakti Peeta's display is on Temple Pillars, and a Yagna Shala is also part of the complex.

Men are encouraged to wear dhoti, kurta or other decent Indian attire; women are advised to wear sarees, salwar kameez or other traditional dresses. In addition, the Sangameswara and Papanasi temples are located within a distance of 2 kms from the Navabrahma temples. The architecture of these temples is exceptional, though it has been ravaged by time and history. All these temples were built by Chalukya kings between the 7 and 11 centuries. The Papanasi temples are a group of temples that were relocated at Alampur from areas that were expected to be submerged after the completion of Srisailam dam. Alampur is situated in Telangana state, and about 200kms from Hyderabad and 22 kms from Kurnool. All the temples of Alampur are located within a radius of 2 kms. It is one of the 18 revered Shakti Peethas in India and has a truly divine and peaceful atmosphere that leaves a lasting impression on devotees and visitors alike. The temple showcases beautiful Chalukyan-era architecture and has a rich historical significance. Surrounding the main shrine are nine ancient Shiva temples, adding to the spiritual charm of the place. The confluence of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers is also nearby, where visitors can enjoy boating while taking in the scenic surroundings. Overall, it is a must-visit destination for anyone interested in history, architecture, and spirituality.'

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: Where is Sri Jogulamba Devi Temple located?
faq.answer: The temple is located in Alampur, Jogulamba Gadwal District, Telangana, near the confluence of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: Which deity is worshipped in the temple?
faq.answer: The temple is dedicated to Goddess Jogulamba, a fierce manifestation of Goddess Parvati, and is one of the 18 Maha Shakti Peethas.
faq.id: FAQ003
faq.question: Why is Jogulamba Temple famous?
faq.answer: It is famous for being one of the 18 Maha Shakti Peethas and for its close association with the ancient Navabrahma Temples and Bala Brahmeswara Swamy Temple.
faq.id: FAQ004
faq.question: What are the temple timings?
faq.answer: The temple generally remains open from 6:30 AM to 8:30 PM, with a break between 1:00 PM and 2:00 PM. Sharannavaratri and other festival days have extended hours.
faq.id: FAQ005
faq.question: Is there an entry fee for darshan?
faq.answer: No. General darshan is free for all devotees. Charges apply only for special sevas and poojas.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Sanghi Temple
Temple ID: T0010
Section: overview

overview: Sri Sanghi Temple, officially Sanghi Temple Devasthanam, is situated atop the picturesque hillock of Paramananda Giri in Sanghi Nagar, Ranga Reddy district, Telangana, approximately 35 km from Hyderabad. Visitors are welcomed by a grand Maha Dwaram and a towering Raja Gopuram visible from several kilometers away. An outstanding example of Chola-Chalukya architecture in pristine white marble, designed by Padma Shri sculptor Sri Ganapathy Sthapathy, the temple was built by the Sanghi family and inaugurated in 1991. Dedicated to Lord Venkateswara, the complex houses numerous shrines and is one of the most visited spiritual destinations in Telangana, drawing lakhs of devotees annually.
summary: Sri Sanghi Temple, atop Paramananda Giri in Sanghi Nagar, Ranga Reddy district, Telangana (~35 km from Hyderabad), is a Chola-Chalukya style temple complex in white marble dedicated to Lord Venkateswara. Built by the Sanghi family with the blessings of Jagadguru Sri Jayendra Saraswathi Shankaracharya of Kanchipuram and designed by Padma Shri sculptor Sri Ganapathy Sthapathy, it was constructed in 18 months and inaugurated in 1991. The complex features a towering Raja Gopuram, a Maha Dwaram, shrines to Padmavathi, Ashtalakshmi, Shiva-Kamalambika, Rama-Sita-Lakshmana-Hanuman, Vijayaganapathi, Kartikeya, Durga, Navagrahas and Hanuman, plus a Pavitra Vanam and Kalyana Mandapam. It sees exceptional footfall on Ekadashi and New Year's Day.

history.section: Foundation & Construction
history.content: The origins of Sanghi Temple date back to 1990, when the Sanghi family envisioned creating a magnificent spiritual centre. With the blessings of Jagadguru Sri Jayendra Saraswathi Shankaracharya of Kanchipuram and under the guidance of Shri Ram Sharan Sanghi and Smt. Kamala Rani Sanghi, the project was spearheaded by Shri Ravi Sanghi and Smt. Anita Sanghi. Construction commenced in 1990 and was completed in just 18 months, culminating in the inauguration of the temple in 1991. Since then it has become one of the most visited spiritual destinations in Telangana, attracting lakhs of devotees annually.

Temple: Sri Sanghi Temple
Temple ID: T0010
Section: architecture

architecture: An outstanding example of Chola-Chalukya architecture designed by renowned sculptor and Padma Shri awardee Sri Ganapathy Sthapathy. The complex is constructed predominantly from pristine white marble and features intricate carvings depicting Hindu mythology and divine beings. Three majestic Gopurams — dedicated to Lord Venkateswara, Goddess Parvathi and Lord Shiva — adorn the foothills of Paramananda Giri. A long flight of steps leads visitors to the complex through an ornately carved entrance, in a style that seamlessly blends South Indian and Dravidian influences.

reviews.top_reviews: Tripadvisor (rimjhim, 2/5, 'Not at all maintained!'): 'We went to Sanghi Temple yesterday as a part of a family outing. The timings on the internet were mentioned as 8:30 to 10:30 AM and 4 PM to 6 PM so we rushed to reach there on time in the evening. The road to the temple is quite nice. It doesn't feel as if you are in Hyderabad as there is greenery on both sides. The entrance hoarding to the temple showed different timings. Its open in the evenings from 4 PM TO 8 PM contrary to what is mentioned on the web and on Sundays it is open from 8AM to 8PM. The temple is not well maintained at all. The grass and greenery that was there a few years back is no longer there. There were muddy patches everywhere and very little of grass. No floral plants as seen a few years back. So the only so called beauty is in terms of the temple structure. The priests seemed highly reluctant to do any kind of 'free' service like offering teertham, flowers etc. It was a major put off. We stayed there till 5:30pm and there was no light in the sanctum sanctorum which was dark inside and made it difficult to see the idols. Very demotivated temple staff. The temple has quite some numbers of monkeys around which are a nuisance. They kept coming near us when we were seated on the benches, forcing us to leave the seats. Overall it was a disappointment. The only plus point was the weather. There's no point driving to the outskirts of the city to see a barren temple land

It is in Koheda Village about 8 Kms from the National Highway between Hyderabad and Vijayawada. The sacred Raja Gopuram, which is very tall, can be seen from several kilometers away. The temple complex is located on the top of Paramanand Giri hill, which attracts a number of devotees who seek the Gods' blessings. The beauty of the slope around the temple is a popular view among its visitors. There are many small temples in the complex but the main temple is Lord Venkateswara. The idol of Venkateshwara inside the sanctum sanctorum is 9-½ ft tall. Timings of Sanghi Temple for public is from 08.00 a.m. to 12.00 noon and from 4.00 p.m.to 8.00 pm. This temple is considered to be a main attraction of Hyderabad.'

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: Where is Sanghi Temple located?
faq.answer: Sanghi Temple is atop Paramananda Giri in Sanghi Nagar, Ranga Reddy district, Telangana, approximately 35 km from Hyderabad.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: Which deity is worshipped at Sanghi Temple?
faq.answer: The presiding deity is Lord Venkateswara (Balaji), whose ~9.5-foot idol is modeled after the deity at Tirumala. The complex also houses shrines to Padmavathi, Ashtalakshmi, Shiva-Kamalambika, Rama, Vijayaganapathi, Kartikeya, Durga, Navagrahas and Hanuman.
faq.id: FAQ003
faq.question: What are the temple timings?
faq.answer: Monday–Saturday: 8:00 AM–1:00 PM and 4:00 PM–8:00 PM. Sundays, public holidays and festival days: 8:00 AM–8:00 PM.
faq.id: FAQ004
faq.question: When was Sanghi Temple built?
faq.answer: Construction began in 1990 and the temple was inaugurated in 1991, completed in 18 months by the Sanghi family.
faq.id: FAQ005
faq.question: Who designed Sanghi Temple's architecture?
faq.answer: The temple was designed by renowned sculptor and Padma Shri awardee Sri Ganapathy Sthapathy in the Chola-Chalukya style.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Kaleshwara Mukteswara Swamy Devasthanam
Temple ID: T0007
Section: overview

overview: Sri Kaleshwara Mukteswara Swamy Temple, popularly known as Kaleshwaram Temple, is one of the most ancient and revered Shiva temples in Telangana. Situated at Kaleshwaram in Jayashankar Bhupalpally district, it stands at the Triveni Sangamam — the confluence of the Godavari, Pranahita and the mystical Saraswati rivers. The temple is uniquely dedicated to two Shiva Lingas, Lord Mukteswara and Lord Kaleshwara, installed together on a single pedestal, a feature believed to symbolise liberation (Moksha) and protection from the cycle of birth and death. Devotees from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh visit throughout the year for health, prosperity, spiritual growth and salvation.
summary: Sri Kaleshwara Mukteswara Swamy Temple at Kaleshwaram, Jayashankar Bhupalpally district, Telangana, is an ancient Shiva temple famed for its unique twin Shiva Lingas (Mukteswara and Kaleshwara) on a single pedestal and its location at the Triveni Sangamam of the Godavari, Pranahita and mystical Saraswati rivers. Dating back over a thousand years and flourishing under the Kakatiya dynasty, it is associated with the legend that Lord Yama installed the Kaleshwara Linga. The Mukteswara Linga has two nostril-like holes through which abhishekam water is believed to flow into the Sangamam. It is a major centre for Moksha-seeking worship, ancestral rituals (Pitru Karmas), and the grand Maha Shivaratri festival.

history.section: Ancient Origin & Kakatiya Patronage
history.content: The temple's history dates back more than a thousand years and is closely associated with ancient Shaivite traditions. Historical records suggest it flourished during the rule of the Kakatiya dynasty, whose kings constructed and renovated several Shiva temples across the Telugu region. Over the centuries the temple has undergone multiple renovations while preserving its original spiritual significance.
history.foundation_year: Over 1,000 years (flourished under the Kakatiya dynasty)
history.founders: Kakatiya dynasty (flourished/renovated)
history.legends: The temple is named for its twin deities — Mukteswara (giver of liberation) and Kaleshwara (associated with time and death).
history.legends: Two Shiva Lingas on a single pedestal are found only at Kaleshwaram.
history.section: Yama Legend
history.content: According to temple legends, Lord Yama, the God of Death, installed the Shiva Linga of Lord Kaleshwara at this sacred site after worshipping Lord Mukteswara to seek liberation from the burden of taking away human lives. Because Lord Yama himself performed penance here, devotees believe worshipping at Kaleshwaram frees them from the fear of death and grants spiritual liberation.
history.legends: Lord Yama installed the Kaleshwara Shiva Linga after worshipping Lord Mukteswara to be freed from the burden of taking human lives.
history.legends: Worship here is believed to free devotees from the fear of death.

The two lingas — Mukteswara (liberation) and Kaleshwara (time and death) — share a single pedestal, unique to this temple. The Mukteswara Linga bears two nostril-like holes through which abhishekam water is believed to flow down into the Triveni Sangamam beneath the temple, a phenomenon regarded as divine. Temple ID: T0007
Section: significance

religious_significance: Kaleshwaram is one of the holiest Shiva temples, where devotees seek blessings for long life, freedom from sins, peace and ultimate liberation (Moksha). The worship of Mukteswara and Kaleshwara together symbolises divine grace and liberation from worldly attachments. The Triveni Sangamam (Godavari, Pranahita and the mythical Saraswati) makes a holy dip here highly meritorious, and the site is a major centre for ancestral rituals (Pitru Karmas).
spiritual_significance: The temple's most distinctive feature is the twin Shiva Lingas on a single pedestal, found nowhere else. The Mukteswara Linga has two nostril-like holes through which abhishekam water is believed to flow into the Triveni Sangamam beneath the temple. Devotees believe a holy dip at the Sangamam before darshan washes away sins, and that performing Pitru Karmas (ancestral rituals) at the confluence brings peace to departed souls and blessings to families. Worship is believed to free devotees from the fear of death and grant Moksha.
healing_beliefs: Freedom from the fear of death and grant of spiritual liberation (Moksha)
healing_beliefs: Long life and freedom from sins

Section: architecture

architecture: The temple showcases a blend of ancient South Indian temple architecture and the artistic excellence of the Kakatiya period. Located on the banks of the Triveni Sangamam, it features beautifully carved stone pillars, traditional mandapams, and a towering Rajagopuram. The sanctum houses the unique twin Shiva Lingas — Lord Mukteswara and Lord Kaleshwara — on a single pedestal, the only such arrangement in India. The complex includes shrines to Goddess Parvati, Lord Ganesha, Lord Subrahmanya, Nandi and other deities, and a separate Saraswathi Ammavari Temple.

Men generally wear dhoti, kurta or other traditional Indian clothing; women are advised to wear sarees, salwar kameez or other decent traditional dresses. Footwear must be removed before entering, silence should be maintained in the sanctum, and photography may be restricted in certain areas.

travel_tips: Carry your own pooja items (coconut, flowers, agarbatties) — shops at the ghat may charge high rates (per Tripadvisor review).
travel_tips: Boating on the river is available and recommended (per Tripadvisor reviews).
travel_tips: Mobile cameras should not be used inside to preserve sanctity (per Tripadvisor reviews).

reviews.top_reviews: Tripadvisor (BAPrakashReddy, 5/5, 'A HOLY -- KALESHWARAM TEMPLE'): 'Visit the temple early mornings for a quicker darshan, prasad is served fresh, there are authorized locker facilities and shoe keepers outside. Abstain from from using mobile cameras to preserve sanctity inside. An important religious town in Karimnagar district of Telangana province adjoining Maharashtra and Adilabad province has Lord Shiva as its main deity. Before entering the temple the devotees takes a holy bath at the river and do the pooja for river. There are 2 siva lingas are placed in the single base in which one is shiva and the another one is yama(god of death). Most of the water comes from pranahita during non rainy season also. Even in summer also the water flow is around 15 to 20 fts in the middle of the river. Boating also available for both the ends.'

reviews.top_reviews: Tripadvisor (Sujeet N C, 5/5, 'Kaleshwaram Temple'): 'An important religious town in Karimnagar district of Telangana province adjoining Maharashtra and Adilabad province has Lord Shiva as its main deity. Rivers Godavari, Pranahita and another tributary join here which is considered auspicious and unique as much as the presence of 2 Shiva Lingas. Lord Yama is also revered here along with Lord Shiva. Temple: Visit early mornings for a quicker darshan, prasad is served fresh, there are authorized locker facilities and shoe keepers outside. Desist from using mobile cameras to preserve sanctity inside. Place: Serene, windy banks on the river front, well preserved environs and forests. Food: Not the best you may expect, small places serving hot puri curry in mornings, South Indian thali at lunch and dinner. So stock up on home made food beforehand. People: Friendly, all religions and faiths live together. Precautions: Take enough cash beforehand as no ATMs there, make sure enough fuel in your vehicle as no fuel stations in a radius of 30 km. Constructive criticism: Authorities need to curtail VIP visits causing inconvenience to common people in the temple, establish at least 1 ATM and 1 fuel station, construct good flooring around the temple environs for smooth walking, establish parks instead of permitting new constructions in the town area. This will help towards making this a neat place for visiting public and preserve the historic importance for the deities.'

reviews.top_reviews: Tripadvisor (Anonymous, 4/5): 'Temple has become so commercial. Priest will be busy serving rich devotees. There is no priest inside the temple during afternoon to give aarti, teerth. Devotees struggle to understand where is the entry is, as there are no proper sign boards. Two laddus in a single pack are sold for Rs.50. pulihora is available in the morning only at Rs.15. Around 30 beggars wait at the entrance/exit to make you inconvenient. Talanilalu is not associated with temple. It's done at the godavari river bank. It's syndicate, no ticket and the rate is fixed Rs.300. The water at the river bank is all dirty with left over clothes and priests left pinda pradaans, coconuts etc. Prefer carrying coconut, flowers and agarbatties from home itself or you will end up paying high. Bus stand is at a walkable distance from temple. Sign boards are proper for rooms booking place.'

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: Where is Sri Kaleshwara Mukteswara Swamy Temple located?
faq.answer: The temple is located in Kaleshwaram village, Jayashankar Bhupalpally district, Telangana, near the Triveni Sangamam.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: Which deity is worshipped in the temple?
faq.answer: The temple is dedicated to Lord Mukteswara and Lord Kaleshwara, two Shiva Lingas installed on a single pedestal.
faq.id: FAQ003
faq.question: What is special about Kaleshwaram Temple?
faq.answer: It is famous for its unique twin Shiva Lingas on a single pedestal and its location at the confluence of the Godavari, Pranahita and the mystical Saraswati rivers (Triveni Sangamam).
faq.id: FAQ004
faq.question: What are the temple timings?
faq.answer: The temple is generally open from 4:00 AM to 1:00 PM and 3:00 PM to 8:30 PM, though timings may vary during festivals.
faq.id: FAQ005
faq.question: Is there an entry fee for darshan?
faq.answer: No. General darshan is free, while special sevas and rituals require separate tickets.

Section: overview

overview: Surendrapuri — Kunda Satyanarayana Kaladhamam, located at the foothills of Yadagirigutta in Yadadri-Bhuvanagiri District, Telangana, is India's first mythological theme park and religious tourism destination, spread over 17 acres. Opened to the public in May 2003 by Sri Kunda Satyanarayana (in memory of his late son Surendra), the complex features 3,000+ sculptures across a 3-km pathway, organised into four categories: Temples of India (life-size replicas of 100+ famous Indian temples), Epics of India (Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata, Buddha Charita), Puranas (Ksheera Sagara Madhanam, Gajendra Moksham, Padmavyuham, Kurukshetra War, etc.), and Saptalokas (the 7 celestial worlds — Brahmalok, Vishnulok, Shivalok, Nagalok, Indralok, Narakalok/Yamalok, Patalalok). The complex also houses the Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam (16-foot black-stone Panchamukha Hanuman from Kanchi + Mahashivalinga similar to Pasupatinath Nepal), 9 Navagraha Temples (each planet with its consort and vahana in dedicated temples), Nagakoti (a 101-foot Shivalinga atop Nagadri Hill encircled by Kaalasarpa with 10 million small anthill-mud Shivalingas), and Surendrapuri's iconic 60-foot double-sided Panchamukha Hanuman-Shiva statue at the entrance. ~60 km from Hyderabad; 10 km from Bhuvanagiri Railway Station; 2 km from Yadadri Bus Terminal. history.section: Founder & Personal Motivation
history.content: Surendrapuri was conceptualized and built by Sri Kunda Satyanarayana, who was born in a small village near Khammam (Telangana) in an agricultural family whose modest means did not allow him to pursue a formal higher education. The sudden passing away of his youngest son, Surendra Babu, aroused in Sri Satyanarayana a desire to build something to keep his memory alive. The idea of a mythological park seemed apt due to his deep abiding love for Indian culture and traditions. He was confronted by daunting challenges — advancing age, huge project costs, and the dissuasion of friends and associates. All the deterrents only served to firm his resolve. At the age of 70, when people have generally retired, he worked doubly hard to bring his dream project to life. After over a decade of dedicated hard work and single-minded commitment, Surendrapuri took concrete shape. Today it stands as a testament to one man's vision, determination and never-say-die attitude.
history.foundation_year: Surendrapuri opened to the public in May 2003; the Kunda Satyanarayana Kaladhamam (the mythological museum) was inaugurated in February 2009 by the then-Governor of Andhra Pradesh, Narayan Dutt Tiwari

sthala_puranam: Surendrapuri does not have a traditional Sthala Puranam as it is a modern mythological theme park and religious tourism destination. The site's sacred character is derived from the 100+ life-size replicas of India's most revered temples (including Tirumala Balaji, Madurai Meenakshi, Kashi Viswanath, Rameswaram, Jagannath Puri, Golden Temple Amritsar, Somnath, Kedarnath, Guruvayur), the sculpted depictions of key events from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata, the life of Buddha, and key events from the Puranas (Ksheera Sagara Madhanam / churning of the ocean, Gajendra Moksham, Padmavyuham, Kurukshetra War, etc.), and the 7 celestial Saptalokas (Brahmalok, Vishnulok, Shivalok, Nagalok, Indralok, Narakalok/Yamalok, Patalalok). The complex also houses the Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam (the protective avatara of Hanuman who killed the 5 bees that hid Mahi Ravan's life), the 101-foot Nagakoti Shivalinga (with 10 million small anthill-mud Shivalingas for Naga Dosha, Kuja Dosha and Kaalasarpa Dosha remedies), and the 9 Navagraha Temples. Surendrapuri is named after Sri Kunda Satyanarayana's son Surendra Babu, and the Kaladhamam is named after Sri Satyanarayana himself.

religious_significance: Surendrapuri is significant in three ways: (1) as India's first mythological theme park, providing an educational and devotional experience of Hindu epics, Puranas, and Saptalokas through 3,000+ sculptures across a 3-km pathway; (2) as a religious-tourism destination housing multiple temples, including the Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam (with a 16-foot Panchamukha Hanuman from Kanchi and a Mahashivalinga similar to the Pasupatinath in Nepal), 9 Navagraha Temples (each planet with its consort and vahana), and the 101-foot Nagakoti Shivalinga; and (3) as a 'tirth yatra' in a single place — visitors can see life-size replicas of 100+ of India's most famous temples in one visit. It is highly relevant for planetary dosha remedies (Naga Dosha, Kuja Dosha, Kaalasarpa Dosha at Nagakoti; planetary shanti at Navagraha Temples) and for protective worship (Panchamukha Hanuman). It is usually visited in conjunction with the famous Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Temple at Yadagirigutta (3 km away), forming a popular weekend pilgrimage from Hyderabad.

spiritual_significance: Devotees believe that the 16-foot Panchamukha Hanuman at the temple protects them from evil and grants courage. The Panchamukha avatara is especially worshipped for protection from black magic, evil eye, and negative energies (since Hanuman, in this form, killed the 5 bees that hid Mahi Ravan's life — defeating all 5 forms of evil simultaneously). The 101-foot Nagakoti Shivalinga, encircled by Kaalasarpa, is believed to be so powerful that just by pradakshina (circumambulation) one can attain salvation from the ill-effects of Naga Dosha, Kuja Dosha and Kaalasarpa Dosha. The 9 Navagraha Temples are believed to mitigate the negative effects of planetary positions on a devotee's horoscope. The 10 million small anthill-mud Shivalingas at Nagakoti are believed to carry the divine energy of the main 101-foot Shivalinga. Many devotees also visit Surendrapuri as a comprehensive 'temple tour of India' — a unique way to gain familiarity with India's diverse temple architecture and mythology in a single visit.

Temple ID: T0022
Section: architecture

architecture: Surendrapuri is built across 17 acres of land, with a 3-km pathway marked by arrows that visitors follow in sequence. The architecture is a unique blend of devotional art, museum display, and temple construction. The complex is divided into multiple zones: (1) The 3-km main pathway inside the Kaladhamam (mythological museum) housing 3,000+ sculptures in 4 categories (Temples of India, Epics of India, Puranas, Saptalokas) — some open air, some indoor depending on size and scene; (2) The Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam — a Vaastu- and Agama-compliant temple with North-South blended Gopuras, housing the 16-foot Panchamukha Hanuman (black stone from Kanchi) and the Mahashivalinga; (3) The 9 Navagraha Temples — each painted in the colour of the principal deity, with the Navagraha, its consort, and vahana installed; (4) The 101-foot Nagakoti Shivalinga atop Nagadri Hill, encircled by Kaalasarpa with 10 million small anthill-mud Shivalingas; (5) The 60-foot double-sided Panchamukha Hanuman-Shiva statue at the entrance. Descriptions in Telugu and English accompany every exhibit, making the complex accessible to all.
architectural_style: Mixed: museum display (open-air + indoor) + Vaastu- and Agama-compliant temples (North-South Gopura blend) + colossal 60-foot and 101-foot statues + 9 individual Navagraha temples + life-size replicas of 100+ famous Indian temples

dress_code: Traditional and modest attire is recommended. Per general Telugu temple convention, men often wear dhoti (and may remove the shirt at the inner sanctums); women wear sarees or salwar suits. Footwear is removed at all temple entrances. For the Kaladhamam pathway (museum), casual but modest attire is acceptable. Carrying umbrellas and protection from heat/rain is recommended (per Telangana360 — the area is largely open-air). Photography is prohibited inside the museum pathway.

travel_tips: Plan to spend at least 2–3 hours inside the Kaladhamam (3-km pathway) to see all 3,000+ sculptures.

travel_tips: Carry water and an umbrella; the pathway is largely open-air and Telangana's heat can be intense.

travel_tips: Wear comfortable footwear (which you'll remove at temple entrances).
travel_tips: Combine with the Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Temple at Yadagirigutta (3 km away) for a half-day pilgrimage from Hyderabad.
travel_tips: Don't consume alcoholic drinks or non-vegetarian food in the temple surroundings (per the Yadagirigutta temple area rules that apply here too).
travel_tips: Switch off your mobile phones at the temples; don't carry weapons or head gear (helmets, caps, turbans) inside the temple premises.
travel_tips: Online ticket booking is available via the official website's Razorpay links (BOOK NOW).
travel_tips: Visit on a weekday morning to avoid the biggest crowds (weekends and holidays are busiest).

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: What is Surendrapuri — Kunda Satyanarayana Kaladhamam?
faq.answer: Surendrapuri is India's first mythological theme park and religious tourism destination, spread over 17 acres in Yadadri-Bhuvanagiri District, Telangana, at the foothills of Yadagirigutta. Opened in May 2003 by Sri Kunda Satyanarayana (in memory of his son Surendra), the complex features 3,000+ sculptures across a 3-km pathway in 4 categories: Temples of India (life-size replicas of 100+ famous Indian temples), Epics of India (Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata, Buddha Charita), Puranas, and Saptalokas (7 celestial worlds). It also houses the Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam (16-foot Panchamukha Hanuman + Mahashivalinga), 9 Navagraha Temples, the 101-foot Nagakoti Shivalinga, and a 60-foot double-sided Panchamukha Hanuman-Shiva statue at the entrance.

Temple ID: T0022
Section: faq

faq.answer: The presiding deity is the 16-foot Panchamukha Hanuman (a five-faced protective avatara of Hanuman), carved from black stone specially brought from Kanchi. The Panchamukha Hanuman has 5 faces (Vanara, Narasimha, Garuda, Varaha, Hayagreeva) and holds 10 different weapons. He manifested this form to kill the 5 bees that hid the life of Mahi Ravan (Ravana's brother), saving Ram and Lakshman. Lord Venkateswara and Goddess Lakshmi are also worshipped in the Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam complex. The complex also includes a Mahashivalinga of Panchamukha Parameswara (similar to Pasupatinath, Nepal).

faq.answer: The 3-km Kaladhamam pathway is divided into 4 categories: (1) Temples of India — life-size replicas of 100+ famous Indian temples including Tirumala Balaji, Madurai Meenakshi, Kashi Viswanath, Shirdi Saibaba, Kolkata Kali, Rameswaram, Jagannath Puri, Golden Temple (Amritsar), Somnath, Kedarnath, Guruvayur, and many more; (2) Epics of India — scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata, and Buddha Charita; (3) Puranas — Ksheera Sagara Madhanam (churning of the ocean), Gajendra Moksham, Padmavyuham, Kurukshetra War, Pralayakalam, Shiva-Parvathi Kalyam, etc.; (4) Saptalokas — the 7 celestial worlds (Brahmalok, Vishnulok, Shivalok, Nagalok, Indralok, Yamalok/Narakalok, Patalalok) with audio-visual effects. There are 3,000+ sculptures in total, both open-air and indoor depending on the size of the replica.

faq.answer: The Nagakoti is a 101-foot Shivalinga situated atop the Nagadri Hill, encircled by the giant snake Kaalasarpa, with 10 million small Shivalingas made from anthill mud. It is believed to be so powerful that just by pradakshina (circumambulation) one can attain salvation from the ill-effects of Naga Dosha, Kuja Dosha, and Kaalasarpa Dosha. Special pujas (Kalasarpa dosha, Naga dosha, Kuja dosha, Parihara poojalu) are performed here. Open 8:30 AM – 5:30 PM daily.
faq.id: FAQ007
faq.question: How much time do I need at Surendrapuri?
faq.answer: The 3-km Kaladhamam pathway takes 2-3 hours to walk through completely (per Tripadvisor reviews). With the temples (Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara, 9 Navagraha, Nagakoti), plan for at least half a day. Most pilgrims combine Surendrapuri with the Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Temple at Yadagirigutta (3 km away) for a half-day pilgrimage from Hyderabad.

page_content:
Temple: Surendrapuri — Kunda Satyanarayana Kaladhamam
Temple ID: T0022
Section: faq

faq.answer: Surendrapuri was designed and built by Sri Kunda Satyanarayana, who was born in a small village near Khammam in an agricultural family. The sudden passing away of his youngest son, Surendra Babu, motivated him to build a memorial that would keep his son's memory alive. The park is named after Surendra. At the age of 70, after facing dissuasion from friends and associates, he worked doubly hard to bring his dream project to life. After over a decade of dedicated work, Surendrapuri was opened to the public in May 2003. The Kunda Satyanarayana Kaladhamam (the mythological museum) was inaugurated in February 2009 by the then-Governor of Andhra Pradesh, N.D. Tiwari.
faq.id: FAQ009
faq.question: How do I reach Surendrapuri?
faq.answer: By road: ~60 km from Hyderabad (1.5 hours drive via NH 163 / NH 365 on the Hyderabad–Warangal highway). TSRTC provides several buses (40-60 min on weekdays, 30-45 min on weekends). By rail: nearest railway station is Raigir (~8 km). By air: nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~88 km). For most visitors, the typical route is Hyderabad → Bhongir → Yadadri Road → Surendrapuri, often combined with the Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Temple at Yadagirigutta (3 km away).

faq.question: What are the special pujas at the Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam?
faq.answer: Special pujas include: (1) Suprabhataseva — early-morning waking ritual; (2) Manyusuktham Sahashodhopachara Puja — special 1008-item offering puja; (3) Panchamutranijabishekam — five-sacred-substance abhishekam; (4) Manyusuktham Parayanam — Vedic hymn recitation. At the Navagraha Temples, special graha-dosha pujas, homas, and Navagraha Homa (eradication of evil) are performed. At Nagakoti, parihara poojas (Kaalasarpa, Naga, Kuja) are performed. Specific fees are not published in the user source; contact the temple office via the official website's GET IN TOUCH link.

faq.answer: Yes — it's an excellent family destination. Children below 5 years enter free; the Kaladhamam is widely praised as 'a great place to teach kids about Hindu mythology and culture' (per JustDial reviews). The pathway is wheelchair-accessible. However, the 3-km walk can be tiring for young children or elderly visitors — plan to take breaks. The pathway is largely open-air, so bring water and an umbrella. Photography is restricted inside the museum, so don't promise kids they can take photos.

best_time_to_visit: October to March is the most pleasant weather window. Special days: Hanuman Jayanti (March/April), Maha Shivaratri (Feb/March), and weekends (especially Sundays). For the most comfortable experience, visit on a weekday morning. The 3-km pathway takes 2–3 hours to walk through completely; plan for at least half a day. Carry water and an umbrella, as much of the pathway is open-air. Avoid peak summer (April–June) due to the heat. Most pilgrims combine Surendrapuri with the Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Temple at Yadagirigutta (3 km away) for a half-day trip from Hyderabad.

page_content:
Temple: Ramappa Temple
Temple ID: T0014
Section: overview

overview: Ramappa Temple, officially the Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, is a magnificent 13th-century Shiva temple at Palampet village, Venkatapur Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana. Constructed between 1212 and 1234 CE (construction began 1213 CE), it is the main Shiva temple in a walled complex built during the Kakatiya period under rulers Rudradeva and Recharla Rudra, and is rare among Indian temples in being named after its chief sculptor, Ramappa. Built of red sandstone, carved granite and dolerite, with a distinctive pyramidal Vimana (stepped tower) made of lightweight porous 'floating bricks' that reduce the roof's weight, it is celebrated for its intricate carvings, the 'Salabhanjikas / Madanika' bracket figures, and the 6-foot-high star-shaped platform. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 25 July 2021 (reference 1570, India's 39th WHS, 44th session), it is geographically and administratively separate from the Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamakonda (~75 km away).

summary: Ramappa Temple (Kakatiya Rudreshwara Temple) at Palampet, Mulugu District, Telangana, is a 13th-century Kakatiya Shiva temple and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 25 July 2021, ref 1570). Construction began in 1213 CE under Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva, commissioned by his general Recharla Rudra, and is named after its sculptor Ramappa. Built of red sandstone, granite, dolerite and lightweight 'floating bricks' on a star-shaped platform, it has survived multiple earthquakes thanks to advanced Kakatiya engineering. It is the ACTUAL UNESCO World Heritage Site — not the Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamakonda (~75 km away), which is only on UNESCO's tentative list. The temple is surrounded by the Ramappa Cheruvu (Kakatiya-built reservoir) and is celebrated for the 'Salabhanjikas' dancing-girl bracket figures.

history.section: Construction & Naming
history.content: The Ramappa Temple complex was constructed between 1212 and 1234 CE (construction began 1213 CE) during the reign of the Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva. It was commissioned by his military commander Recharla Rudra (also rendered Recharla Rudra Reddy). The temple is unusual in being named after its chief sculptor/architect, Ramappa, rather than its presiding deity (the deity is Ramalingeshwara Swamy, a form of Shiva). Marco Polo, during his visit to the Kakatiya empire, supposedly called the temple 'the brightest star in the galaxy of temples'. The temple faces east and is approached by a long flight of stairs from the east, north and south. The cornice above the three gateways is supported by black basalt brackets in the shape of dancing girls (Salabhanjikas) — four per gate, totalling 12 — with the remaining brackets representing yallis (mythical lion-elephant hybrids).

history.legends: Marco Polo, on visiting the Kakatiya empire, reportedly called the temple 'the brightest star in the galaxy of (medieval Deccan) temples'.
history.section: Preservation, Research & UNESCO Recognition
history.content: Despite surviving several earthquakes over the centuries, the temple remains remarkably well preserved due to its advanced engineering techniques (sandbox foundation and lightweight 'floating brick' Vimana). Academic research on the temple's engineering began in the 1980s under Prof. M. Panduranga Rao. In 1931 CE, Ghulam Yazdani published 'The Temples at Palampet' (Memoirs of the ASI, No. 6), one of the earliest systematic studies. On 25 July 2021, at the 44th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, the Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural criteria i and iii, reference 1570) — India's 39th World Heritage Site and the first such site in Telangana. The temple is centrally protected and maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) under the AMASR Act, 2010; the buffer zone extends 300 m from the core zone boundary.

religious_significance: Ramappa Temple is an important Shaivite pilgrimage destination in Telangana. Devotees visit to seek the blessings of Lord Shiva (as Ramalingeshwara Swamy) for prosperity, health and spiritual well-being. Beyond its religious role, it is regarded as one of India's greatest architectural achievements, admired by scholars and visitors worldwide.

The temple complex's setting — at the foothills of a forested area and amidst agricultural fields, close to the shores of the Ramappa Cheruvu (a Kakatiya-built reservoir) — follows the ideology and practice sanctioned in dharmic texts that temples are to be constructed to form an integral part of a natural setting (hills, forests, springs, streams, lakes, catchment areas, and agricultural lands).

architecture: Ramappa Temple is built in the Kakatiya architectural style (Kakatiya, Bhumija / Vesara), using red sandstone, black basalt, carved granite and dolerite, with a distinctive pyramidal Vimana (horizontally stepped tower) made of lightweight porous 'floating bricks' that reduce the weight of the roof structures. The central shrine has a star-shaped plan and stands on a 6-foot-high plinth. The temple faces east and is approached by a long flight of stairs from east, north and south. The cornice above the three gateways is supported by black basalt brackets in the shape of dancing girls (Salabhanjikas) — four per gate, totalling 12 — with the remaining brackets representing yallis (mythical lion-elephant hybrids). The interior houses a Shiva Linga in the inner sanctum, entered through an ornamental gateway of shining black basalt. Basalt pillars with intricate ornamentation support the roof of the open space in front of the inner sanctum. The exterior walls have rich relief ornamentations. reviews.top_reviews: The Ramappa Temple, located in Palampet village, Telangana, is a 13th-century UNESCO World Heritage Site dedicated to Lord Shiva. Built between 1213 and 1323 CE, it is renowned for its sandbox foundation, intricate basalt carvings, and lightweight 'floating bricks' used in the spire. It is a premier example of Kakatiya architecture. Inscribed in 2021 as a World Heritage Site, it is the first such site in Telangana. Situated in Palampet, Mulugu district, approximately 200 km from Hyderabad and 66 km from Warangal. Built in 1213 CE by Recherla Rudra, a general of the Kakatiya king Ganapathi Deva, and designed by the sculptor Ramappa. The temple rests on a 'sand-box' foundation, which provides stability during earthquakes. The shikhara (tower) is built with lightweight, porous bricks that float in water. It features intricate carvings on black basalt stone, depicting scenes from Hindu mythology and dance, often referred to as the 'crest jewel' of Kakatiya art. The temple is open to visitors from 6 AM to 6 PM. The temple is also known as the Rudreshwara Temple. Visitors are often advised to take personal transport from Mulugu, as public transport options to Palampet are limited.
reviews.positive_themes: Outstanding Kakatiya architecture

faq.answer: It was commissioned in 1213 CE by the military commander Recharla Rudra (also rendered Recharla Rudra Reddy) during the reign of Kakatiya King Ganapati Deva (r. 1199–1262), and named after its chief sculptor/architect Ramappa. Construction continued for about 40 years (c. 1212–1234 CE).
faq.id: FAQ005
faq.question: Which deity is worshipped here?
faq.answer: Lord Ramalingeshwara Swamy (Lord Shiva) is the presiding deity, represented by a Shiva Linga in the inner sanctum.
faq.id: FAQ006
faq.question: When was Ramappa Temple inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.answer: It was inscribed on 25 July 2021 at the 44th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, as reference 1570 under cultural criteria (i) and (iii). It is India's 39th World Heritage Site and the first in Telangana.

faq.question: Is the Ramappa Temple the same as the Thousand Pillar Temple?

faq.answer: No. They are two distinct Kakatiya monuments. The Ramappa Temple is in Palampet, Mulugu District (~200 km NE of Hyderabad, ~66 km from Warangal), is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021), was built 1213 CE under Ganapati Deva by Recharla Rudra, and is dedicated to Shiva (Ramalingeshwara). The Thousand Pillar Temple is in Hanamakonda, Hanamakonda District (~150 km from Hyderabad), is only on UNESCO's tentative list, was built 1163 CE under Rudra Deva, and is a Trikutalayam of Shiva, Vishnu and Surya. They are about 75 km apart.

faq.answer: Major festivals include Maha Shivaratri, Karthika Masam, Ugadi, Sankranti, Deepavali and Pradosham celebrations.

faq.question: Is photography allowed?
faq.answer: Photography is generally allowed in the temple's exterior areas, subject to ASI rules. No flash inside the sanctum. Respect any restrictions inside protected sections.

faq.answer: Yes. Parking facilities are available near the temple complex.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Sammakka Saralamma Temple (Medaram)
Temple ID: T0021
Section: overview

overview: Sri Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram, in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt), Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana, is the site of Asia's largest tribal religious congregation — the Sammakka Saralamma Jatara (Medaram Jathara), held biennially in honour of the tribal mother-daughter duo Sammakka and Saralamma. Declared a State Festival in 1998, the Jathara draws 1.5–3 crore devotees over four days (next: 28–31 January 2028, with 2026 having just concluded), making it the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. The rituals are performed entirely by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs (no Vedic or Brahmanic influence). Devotees offer 'Bangaram' (jaggery, equal to their weight in some traditions), 'Odi Biyyam' (sacred rice) and take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu (named after the tribal warrior Jampanna, who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army in that stream). The temple complex is administered by a non-hereditary chairman board, with MLA Santosh Chakravarthy having served as the first chairman (appointed 27 April 1968). The Telangana government reconstructed the altars of the deities (Sammakka, Saralamma, Govindaraju, Pagididda Raju) at a cost of ~₹101 crore ahead of the 2026 Jathara, with additional ₹150 crore in development works.

summary: Sri Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram (Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana) is the site of Asia's largest tribal religious congregation, the Sammakka Saralamma Jatara — a biennial State Festival in honour of the tribal mother-daughter goddesses Sammakka and Saralamma. Held every two years in late January (next: 28–31 January 2028), the four-day Jathara draws 1.5–3 crore devotees, making it the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. Rituals are performed entirely by Koya tribe priests (no Vedic/Brahmanic influence). Devotees offer Bangaram (jaggery), take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu (named after the tribal warrior Jampanna), and worship the forest goddesses. The Telangana government spent ~₹101 crore on altar reconstruction and ₹150 crore on development works for 2026, deploying 21 departments, 42,000+ personnel, ~9,000 police, and ~500 NSS volunteers. Until 1955 only ~2,000 people attended, mostly Koya tribals; today the Koya community represents just 2% of the 1.3+ crore pilgrims.

history.section: 13th-century Origin & the Kakatiya Revolt
history.content: Per tribal tradition, the goddess Sammakka and her daughter Saralamma were tribal leaders who lived in the 12th–13th centuries and led a revolt against the Kakatiya rulers' unjust tax on the tribal populace during a prolonged drought. Sammakka was married to Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas (who ruled the country of Andhra from Warangal City between 1000 AD and 1380 AD). She was blessed with 2 daughters and 1 son: Sarakka, Nagulamma and Jampanna respectively. Jampanna was a tribal warrior who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now named Jampanna Vagu after him; the water is reportedly red in colour — scientifically attributed to the soil composition, but tribally believed to be marked with Jampanna's blood). Per tribal legend, it was Sammakka's curse which caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. The Jathara commemorates their sacrifice and is the largest repeating tribal religious congregation in the world.
history.foundation_year: 13th century (per tribal tradition; legend dates back ~700 years)
history.legends: Sammakka was born ~6–7 centuries ago (13th century), when tribal leaders on a hunt found a newborn girl emitting enormous light playing amidst tigers; the head of the tribe adopted and raised her as a chieftain.

history.content: Until 1955, only about 2,000 people visited Medaram, of whom the majority (1,500) belonged to the Koya tribe. In 1946, the Jatara was held with greater fervour and attendance than ever before under the supervision of Subedar Amir Ali Khan, who instituted multiple water stations, first-aid posts, mobile medical units, traffic regulation, sanitation, and crowd management — widely cited as a precedent-setting public welfare effort. Until 1998, the only way to reach Medaram was by bullock cart; in that year, the state government declared the 1,000-year-old festival as official (a State Festival) and laid down a motorable road. MLA Santosh Chakravarthy was appointed as the first chairman of the Sammakka Sarakka Temple on 27 April 1968. In 2008, ~8 million people attended; today attendance is ~10 million+ per cycle. The 2012 Jathara attracted ~1 crore people. page_content:
Temple: Sri Sammakka Saralamma Temple (Medaram)
Temple ID: T0021
Section: history

sthala_puranam: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka was born in the 13th century, found as a newborn emitting enormous light amid tigers, and was adopted by the head of the Koya tribe. She married Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas, and had 2 daughters (Sarakka/Saralamma and Nagulamma) and 1 son (Jampanna). When the Kakatiya rulers imposed an unjust tax on the tribals during a prolonged drought, Sammakka and her daughter Saralamma led a tribal revolt. Jampanna, Sammakka's son and a tribal warrior, died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now Jampanna Vagu after him; the water is still reddish — tribally believed to be marked with his blood). Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. The forest goddesses are believed to 'visit' their devotees during the biennial Jathara, after which they return to the forest (Vana Pravesham) — the focal point of the four-day festival. The rituals are entirely performed by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs, with no Vedic or Brahmanic influence.

page_content:

Temple ID: T0021
Section: significance

religious_significance: Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram is the site of Asia's largest tribal religious congregation and a State Festival of Telangana (since 1998). It is the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. The temple is a non-Vedic, non-Brahmanic shrine entirely administered by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs. It is a major centre for tribal religious identity, drawing 1.5–3 crore devotees from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand. Devotees offer Bangaram (jaggery), Odi Biyyam (sacred rice), turmeric, vermilion, rice and cloth; women offer sarees; and pilgrims take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu. The temple is revered as a symbol of tribal resistance, women's leadership (Sammakka as a female warrior-chieftain) and forest-deity devotion. The 2026 Jathara was inaugurated by the Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy on 19 January 2026 (reconstructed shrine inauguration).

spiritual_significance: Devotees believe Sammakka and Saralamma are forest goddesses (Devathas) who 'visit' their devotees during the Jathara period and return to the forest after four days (Vana Pravesham). The rituals performed at the gaddelu (sacred altar) are believed to bestow protection, fulfilment of vows (Mokubadulu), and ancestral blessings. Devotees come seeking solutions to personal and family problems, court cases, marital issues, child-related concerns, and protection of tribal lands and forests. The red water of Jampanna Vagu is believed to remind tribals of the sacrifice of their gods and to induce courage in their souls. The festival is a major assertion of tribal cultural identity and continuity, and the journey to Medaram itself is considered a sacred pilgrimage.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Sammakka Saralamma Temple (Medaram)
Temple ID: T0021
Section: architecture

architecture: The Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram has a distinct tribal-Shaivite architecture, blending folk-tribal elements with simple South Indian temple features. The gaddelu (sacred altar) is the focal point of the four-day Jathara, where the deities are ceremonially installed. Saralamma is installed in a temple at Kannepally (a small village near Medaram), and Sammakka is at Chilakala Gutta in the form of a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (a vermilion-form deity — i.e. the goddess is represented by a mound of vermilion rather than a stone or metal idol). The complex is in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt). The Telangana government reconstructed the altars of the deities (Sammakka, Saralamma, Govindaraju, Pagididda Raju) at a cost of ~₹101 crore ahead of the 2026 Jathara. The Jampanna Vagu (a tributary of the Godavari) flows through the forest region, with a bridge constructed on top of it (Jampanna Vagu bridge). The complex includes Forest Tents (100 tents set up by the Forest Department; up to 5 persons per tent; 24-hour/12-hour rentals), Kalyana Katta, Ballon No. 5, and 21 government department-managed facilities.

festivals.festival: Sammakka Saralamma Jatara (Medaram Maha Jathara)
festivals.description: The principal and most significant festival — held biennially over 4 days in late January. The 2026 cycle was 28–31 January 2026; the next cycle is expected January 2028. Asia's largest tribal religious congregation, drawing 1.5–3 crore devotees over the 4-day period — the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. The CM of Telangana (A. Revanth Reddy) inaugurated the reconstructed shrine on 19 January 2026; the 4-day festival itself was 28–31 January 2026, concluding at 7:55 PM on 31 January with Vana Pravesham. The 2026 Jathara deployed 21 government departments, 42,027 personnel, ~9,000 police, hundreds of CCTV cameras, 2 drone cameras, and ~500 NSS volunteers from Kakatiya University.
festivals.festival: Karthika Masam (October–November)
festivals.description: Tribal devotees perform small-scale pujas at the Kannepally and Chilakala Gutta shrines during Karthika Masam (off-Jathara period).
festivals.festival: Magh Purnima / Full Moon days
festivals.description: Per local tradition, the Jathara was historically associated with the full moon (Shuddha Purnima) day, though the modern 4-day Jathara runs Wednesday-to-Saturday in late January.

darshan_and_tickets.general_darshan: Free entry to Medaram and the gaddelu during the Jathara period. No entry ticket is required for the 4-day festival. Outside the Jathara period, the site is in the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary and is generally closed to non-tribal visitors (forest permits may be required for general visits).
darshan_and_tickets.special_darshan: No special darshan or VIP system is documented — the gaddelu is a shared, open platform where all devotees queue for darshan.
darshan_and_tickets.ticket_details: Forest Tent accommodation: ₹2,000 for 24 hours / ₹1,000 for 12 hours (contact: +91 95531 42346 — A. Venkat). All other offerings (Bangaram, Odi Biyyam, sarees, holy dip in Jampanna Vagu) are voluntary. The 2026 government spent ~₹101 crore on altar reconstruction and ₹150 crore on development works.

dress_code: Tribal devotees wear traditional Koya attire. For general pilgrims: traditional and modest attire is recommended — men often wear dhoti (and may remove the shirt at the inner sanctum / gaddelu per Telugu tribal convention); women wear sarees (which is also one of the principal offerings at the Jathara). Footwear is removed at the gaddelu and at the temple area. Pilgrims are advised to wear light, weather-appropriate clothing and to carry water during the crowded 4-day Jathara.

accommodation.availability: Accommodation is severely limited even on Jathara days — most pilgrims stay in Warangal, Hyderabad, or other nearby towns and travel in for the day. On-site: 100 Forest Tents (5 persons/tent); Airbnb options (per medaramjathara.com). The 2026 arrangements emphasised day-pilgrimage with massive bus operations rather than overnight stays at Medaram.
accommodation.booking_process: Forest Tent booking: contact +91 95531 42346 (A. Venkat) on the day or in advance. Airbnb: book via airbnb.co.in (specific Medaram listings exist). Most pilgrims travel from Warangal (~90 km) or Hyderabad (~300 km) for the day.
accommodation.first_come_basis: Forest Tents are on a first-come, first-served basis during the Jathara.
accommodation.price_range: Forest Tents: ₹2,000 for 24 hours / ₹1,000 for 12 hours (per 2026 official rates). Airbnb: variable, typically ₹1,500–₹5,000 per night for private homes around Medaram. Hotels in Warangal (the closest city, ~90 km): ₹800–₹4,000 per night for budget-mid-range.
