travel.road: Medaram is ~90 km from Warangal city. Until 1998, the only way to reach Medaram was by bullock cart; in 1998, the state government laid down a motorable road. For the 2026 Jathara, TSRTC ran nearly 4,000 buses daily to move around 21 lakh people, with 30 bus points to Medaram. Special buses run from all areas of Telangana. From Hyderabad, the route is via Warangal; from Warangal, local buses and special Jathara buses. Buses also connect from Bhupalpally, Kothagudem, Mancherial, Karimnagar, and the surrounding districts. Massive parking areas are set up for the 4-day festival. The official website lists TGSRTC fares (e.g., Godavarikhani 175 km ₹400; Peddapalli 185 km ₹420; Manthani 150 km ₹350; B-Incline 175 km ₹400).
travel.rail: Nearest major railway station is Warangal (~90 km). Kazipet Junction is also a major railhead (~95 km). The Hyderabad + Greater Hyderabad regions together accounted for more than 5.18 lakh bus passengers during the 2026 Jathara, while Warangal zones and Karimnagar region also contributed significantly.
travel.air: Nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~300 km, 5–6 hours by road).
travel.distances: Hyderabad: ~300 km (~5–6 hours by road)
travel.distances: Warangal: ~90 km (the closest major city, base for many pilgrims)

travel_tips: Carry water, light food, comfortable footwear (which you'll remove at the gaddelu and Jampanna Vagu), and a towel for the holy dip.
travel_tips: Bring Bangaram (jaggery) of a quantity equal to your body weight for the principal offering — this is the most auspicious offering.
travel_tips: If you plan to take a holy dip in Jampanna Vagu, do so on Day 3 (the main day for snanams).
travel_tips: Avoid the area in the afternoon of Day 4 (Vana Pravesham) unless you specifically want to witness the return-to-forest procession.
travel_tips: Do not enter Medaram without a forest permit outside the Jathara period — it is in the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt).
travel_tips: Use the TSRTC special buses (4,000 daily) rather than private vehicles during the Jathara; the traffic jam can extend up to 60 km on the Warangal highway.
travel_tips: Take personal responsibility for your belongings — the crowds are massive (up to 3 crore over 4 days).
travel_tips: Use the missing persons camps at key locations if you get separated from family.
travel_tips: Be aware that there are no ATMs or banks at Medaram — carry sufficient cash.

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: What is the Sammakka Saralamma Jatara?
faq.answer: It is a biennial tribal religious festival held in honour of the tribal mother-daughter goddesses Sammakka and Saralamma at Medaram village in Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana. It is recognised as Asia's largest tribal religious congregation, drawing 1.5 to 3 crore devotees over 4 days — the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. Declared a State Festival in 1998, it is performed entirely by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs (no Vedic or Brahmanic influence). The 2026 cycle was 28–31 January 2026; the next is expected January 2028.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: Where is the Sammakka Saralamma Temple located?
faq.answer: In Medaram village, Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana – 506344, India. The temple is in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt), ~90 km from Warangal city and ~300 km from Hyderabad. The gaddelu (sacred altar) is the focal point of the Jathara; the Saralamma temple is in nearby Kannepally; Sammakka's 'Kumkuma Bharina' is at Chilakala Gutta.

faq.answer: Day 1 (Wednesday) — Secret morning pujas at Kannepally; evening 6:00 PM: Saralamma brought to Medaram Gaddhe via Jampanna Vaagu; over 3 million devotees. Day 2 (Thursday) — Edurukolla Ghattam (bamboo-stick ritual); evening 6:00 PM: Sammakka brought from Chilakala Gutta to gaddhe; SP fires 3 gunshots to inaugurate the bali. Day 3 (Friday) — Main day: devotees take Punya Snanams in Jampanna Vaagu; main darshan of Sammakka and Saralamma; offerings of Bangaram, Odi Biyyam, sarees, turmeric, vermilion, rice, cloth. Day 4 (Saturday) — Final darshan; afternoon Ammavarlu Vana Pravesham (return to forest at ~6:00 PM); the 4-day Jathara concludes with religious chants.

Section: faq

faq.answer: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka was born in the 13th century, found as a newborn emitting enormous light amid tigers, adopted by the Koya tribe head. She married Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas, and had 2 daughters (Sarakka/Saralamma, Nagulamma) and 1 son (Jampanna). She led a tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya tax during a drought. Jampanna, her son, died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now Jampanna Vagu). Per legend, Sammakka's curse caused the Kakatiya decline. Saralamma is installed in a temple at Kannepally; Sammakka is at Chilakala Gutta in the form of a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (vermilion form).
faq.id: FAQ007
faq.question: What is the Jampanna Vagu?
faq.answer: Jampanna Vagu is a tributary of the River Godavari that flows through the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary near Medaram. It is named after the tribal warrior Jampanna (Sammakka's son), who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army in that stream. The water is still reddish in colour — tribally believed to be marked with his blood (scientifically attributed to the soil composition). A holy dip (Punya Snanam) in the red waters is central to the Jathara experience. The Jampanna Vagu bridge crosses the stream.

faq.id: FAQ008
faq.question: What is Bangaram and how is it offered?
faq.answer: Bangaram is the local name for jaggery (bellam) — symbolic of gold. It is the most important offering in the Sammakka Sarakka Jathara. Devotees offer jaggery of a quantity equal to their body weight to the goddesses. The offering is part of the Mokubadulu (vow fulfilment) tradition. Other offerings include Odi Biyyam (sacred rice, by women), sarees, turmeric, vermilion, rice and cloth.
faq.id: FAQ009
faq.question: How do I reach Medaram for the Jathara?
faq.answer: By road: ~90 km from Warangal (~2.5–3 hours); ~300 km from Hyderabad (~5–6 hours). TSRTC runs special buses during the Jathara from all areas of Telangana (30+ bus points to Medaram). By rail: nearest major station is Warangal (~90 km). By air: nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~300 km). For the 2026 Jathara, TSRTC ran nearly 4,000 buses daily to move ~21 lakh people. During the Jathara, expect heavy traffic and plan for day-pilgrimage (most pilgrims stay in Warangal or Hyderabad and travel in for the day).

faq.id: FAQ011
faq.question: What should I wear and bring for the Jathara?
faq.answer: Wear traditional attire — men in dhoti (often shirtless at the gaddelu per tribal convention); women in sarees (which is also a principal offering). Carry water, light food, comfortable footwear (which you'll remove at the gaddelu and Jampanna Vagu), a towel for the holy dip, and jaggery (Bangaram) of a quantity equal to your body weight for the principal offering. There are no ATMs or banks at Medaram — carry sufficient cash. Be prepared for massive crowds (up to 40 lakh on Day 3).

Temple ID: T0021

faq.answer: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. After Sammakka and her daughter led the tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya tax during a drought, and after her son Jampanna died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at Jampanna Vagu, the Kakatiya empire gradually declined. The Jathara commemorates this tribal resistance and the sacrifice of Sammakka, Saralamma and Jampanna. It is a major assertion of tribal cultural identity and the memory of the 13th-century tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya rule.

best_time_to_visit: The 4-day Sammakka Saralamma Jatara in late January is the only time most pilgrims visit — next cycle January 2028 (expected 26–29 January 2028). For off-season visitors, October to February is the most pleasant weather window, though the temple is in the deep Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary and may be closed to non-tribal visitors outside the Jathara. Avoid peak days (Day 3 — Friday) if you dislike crowds (up to 40 lakh on the busiest day per 2026 arrangements). Pilgrims are advised to arrive early in the morning, carry water, wear light traditional clothing, and be prepared for significant walking and queueing.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Balaji Venkateswara Swamy Temple
Temple ID: T0008
Section: overview

overview: Chilkur Balaji Temple (Sri Balaji Venkateswara Swamy Temple), popularly known as the 'Visa Balaji Temple', is one of the oldest temples in the Hyderabad/Ranga Reddy region, located at Chilkur Village on the banks of Osman Sagar, off Vikarabad Road. The presiding deity is a Swayambhu (self-manifested) idol of Lord Balaji Venkateswara flanked by Sridevi and Bhoodevi. The temple is uniquely run by hereditary trustees/archakas (Dr. M.V. Soundara Rajan, C.S. Gopala Krishna, and current head priest C.S. Rangarajan) and operates independently of the state Endowments Department. It is celebrated for having no hundi (donation box), accepting no monetary donations, and offering no VIP or paid special darshan — every devotee follows the same queue. Its defining practice is 11 pradakshinas while making a wish and 108 once the wish is fulfilled.

summary: Chilkur Balaji Temple in Ranga Reddy District, Telangana, is a 14th-century (per Wikipedia) Vaishnavite shrine to a Swayambhu idol of Lord Balaji Venkateswara with Sridevi and Bhoodevi. Popularly called 'Visa Balaji' because devotees flock here to pray for overseas visa success, it is one of India's very few trustee-managed temples that won legal autonomy from the state Endowments Department (2008). It charges no fees — no hundi, no donations, no VIP darshan — and its core ritual is the 11/108 pradakshina vow. Principal festival: the seven-day Brahmotsavam in Chaitra (March/April).

history.section: Historical Background
history.content: Chilkur Balaji Temple is regarded as one of the oldest temples in the Hyderabad/Ranga Reddy region. Wikipedia's infobox records the structure as completed in the 14th century, while tourism sources (including the Ranga Reddy District government page) describe it as built 'half a millennium ago'. It is said to have been built during the era of Akkanna and Madanna, ministers under the Qutub Shahi (Golconda) administration and uncles of the Bhakti-poet Ramadas of Bhadrachalam. In 1963, the year following the Sino-Indian border conflict, the idol of the temple's goddess (Ammavaru) was installed and named 'Rajya Lakshmi' to mark the restoration of peace.

history.content: In 2008 the temple won a legal and administrative fight to remain outside the direct control of the state Endowments Department, preserving its independent trustee-managed status — one of very few Hindu temples in India with this standing. In April 2008 it introduced a dress code, requesting handloom clothing on Saturdays to support the handloom weavers of Sircilla. In 2024–2025, following a large turnout during the 2024 Brahmotsavam, the temple began a recurring Friday 'Garuda Prasadam' distribution for devotees seeking blessings for children.

Section: history

history.content: Temple tradition holds that a devotee who regularly visited Tirupati fell seriously ill and could not travel. Lord Venkateswara appeared to him in a dream saying, 'I am right here in the jungle nearby; you do not have to worry.' The devotee went to the spot shown, found a mole-hill and dug into it; his axe accidentally struck a buried idol, causing it to 'bleed', after which a voice instructed him to bathe the mound in cow's milk. Doing so revealed a Swayambhu idol of Lord Balaji flanked by Sridevi and Bhoodevi, and a temple was built to house it.

page_content:

Section: significance

religious_significance: Chilkur Balaji is regarded as an accessible manifestation of Lord Venkateswara ('Pratyaksha Daiva' of the Kali Yuga) for those unable to travel to Tirumala Tirupati. Its defining devotional practice is 11 pradakshinas of the inner shrine while making a wish, followed by 108 pradakshinas once the wish is fulfilled. The temple is distinguished by two verified features: it has no hundi and accepts no monetary donations, and it provides no VIP or expedited darshan — all devotees follow the same queue.
spiritual_significance: The temple's best-known belief is its association with success in visa applications for overseas travel, study or work (hence 'Visa Balaji'). Devotees also seek blessings for employment, marriage and (via the Friday Garuda Prasadam) for children. These are devotional beliefs reported in tourism and news sources; they are not medical, legal, or immigration guarantees.

The complex includes separate shrines for Lord Balaji Venkateswara, Goddess Sridevi, and Goddess Bhoodevi.

Key Reasons for its Fame: Visa Fulfillment (the primary reason for its fame is the strong belief that Lord Balaji grants wishes related to obtaining visas, attracting many hopeful travelers); Unique Rituals (devotees perform 11 pradakshinas around the inner shrine while praying; once their wish is granted, they return to complete 108 pradakshinas as a sign of gratitude); Simplicity & Equality (the temple is known for its simple structure, lack of donation boxes (hundis), and absence of VIP treatment, ensuring all devotees are treated equally); Pratyaksha Daiva (it is considered a powerful, self-manifested deity (Swayambhu) of Lord Venkateswara, accessible to those who cannot visit Tirupati).'

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: Why is Chilkur Balaji Temple called the 'Visa Balaji' or 'Visa Temple'?
faq.answer: Because a large proportion of devotees visit to pray for success in visa applications for overseas travel, study or work, and popular belief holds that the 11-pradakshina vow helps fulfil this wish.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: What are the temple's darshan timings?
faq.answer: The official Telangana Tourism portal lists Monday–Sunday, 5:00 AM–8:00 PM. Independent visitor guides also report a brief mid-afternoon closure (~3:00 PM–3:30 PM) for cleaning; exact timings vary slightly between sources, so confirm on the day, especially during festivals.
faq.id: FAQ003
faq.question: Is there an entry fee or ticket for darshan?
faq.answer: No. Darshan is completely free for all devotees, and the temple does not operate a hundi (donation box) or accept monetary donations.
faq.id: FAQ004
faq.question: Are there any paid special darshans or VIP entry options?
faq.answer: No. The temple treats all devotees equally, with no VIP or expedited darshan of any kind.
faq.id: FAQ005
faq.question: What is the significance of the 11 and 108 pradakshinas?

page_content:
Temple: Sri Balaji Venkateswara Swamy Temple
Temple ID: T0008
Section: faq

faq.answer: Devotees circumambulate the inner shrine 11 times while making a wish (vow). Once the wish is believed fulfilled, they return and perform 108 circumambulations as gratitude.
faq.id: FAQ006
faq.question: Is there a dress code?
faq.answer: General decent/traditional attire is expected. Since April 2008, the temple additionally requests handloom clothing on Saturdays, to support the handloom weavers of Sircilla.
faq.id: FAQ007
faq.question: Can pujas or sevas be booked online?
faq.answer: No online booking or seva-booking portal was found. Darshan and standard worship require no advance booking.
faq.id: FAQ008
faq.question: How do I get to the temple from Hyderabad?
faq.answer: By road via Mehdipatnam and Langar House (~25–33 km); by TSRTC bus route 288D from Mehdipatnam Bus Station; or by taxi/cab from the city or from Rajiv Gandhi International Airport (~20–25 km away).
faq.id: FAQ009
faq.question: Is there a railway station near the temple?
faq.answer: No station is directly adjacent. The nearest major station is Hyderabad Deccan (Nampally), from which onward road transport is required.
faq.id: FAQ010
faq.question: Where can devotees stay near the temple?

faq.question: When is the temple most crowded?
faq.answer: Fridays and Sundays see the heaviest footfall (75,000–1,00,000 devotees reported weekly), increasing further during Poolangi, Annakota and the annual Brahmotsavam.

faq.question: What is the best time of year to visit?
faq.answer: Cooler months from September/October through February/March; avoid peak summer (April–June, when temperatures can exceed 40°C).

page_content:
Temple: Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple
Temple ID: T0013
Section: overview

overview: The Thousand Pillar Temple, officially the Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple and locally called 'Veyyi Stambala Gudi', is a star-shaped Trikutalayam (triple-shrine complex) at the base of Hanamakonda Hill in Hanamakonda, Telangana. Built in 1163 CE by the Kakatiya king Rudra Deva, it took roughly 72 years to complete and is one of the earliest surviving masterpieces of Kakatiya art, architecture and sculpture. The complex, dedicated to Lord Shiva (Rudreshwara, east), Lord Vishnu (south) and Surya Deva (west), features close to 1,000 intricately carved pillars, a monolithic dolerite Nandi, perforated stone screens, rock-cut elephants and a restored Kalyana Mandapam. Centrally protected by the Archaeological Survey of India since 2001, it is on India's UNESCO tentative World Heritage list as part of 'The Glorious Kakatiya Temples and Gateways'. It is geographically and administratively distinct from the Ramappa Temple (UNESCO World Heritage Site 2021) at Palampet in Mulugu District, ~75 km away.

summary: The Thousand Pillar Temple (Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple) is a 1163 CE Kakatiya Trikutalayam at Hanamakonda, Warangal, Telangana, dedicated to Shiva (Rudreshwara), Vishnu and Surya. Built by Kakatiya king Rudra Deva in late Chalukyan / early Kakatiya (Vesara) style using dolerite and granite, it is famed for its ~1,000 carved pillars, monolithic Nandi, and the earthquake-resistant 'sandbox' foundation. It is NOT a UNESCO World Heritage Site — only the Ramappa Temple (Palampet, ~75 km away) carries that designation since 2021. The Thousand Pillar is on UNESCO's tentative list alongside Warangal Fort and Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, and is centrally protected by the ASI.

history.section: Construction & Kakatiya Patronage
history.content: The temple was built in 1163 CE under the patronage of the Kakatiya king Rudra Deva (Rudradeva I), and construction is generally reported to have taken about 72 years (sources commonly cite c. 1175–1324 CE as the broader build/expansion window). It is named after its builder-king as Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple, with the presiding Shiva deity known as Rudreshwara. Successive Kakatiya rulers — Ganapati Deva, Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra — patronised and expanded the complex over the 12th–14th centuries. Per popular temple lore, King Rudra Deva had a divine vision in which Lord Shiva directed him to build a temple with a thousand pillars, each symbolically representing a lingam (this account is recorded in popular/tourism sources rather than a verifiable primary religious text).

page_content:
Temple: Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple
Temple ID: T0013
Section: history

history.content: In the 14th century the temple complex — particularly the Kalyana Mandapam — suffered significant damage during the Deccan invasions of the Delhi Sultanate's Tughlaq dynasty; the core shrines survived due to their massive stone foundations and the Kakatiya 'sandbox' foundation technique. In the early 20th century, Mir Osman Ali Khan, the seventh Nizam of Hyderabad, contributed a grant (~₹1 lakh) toward reconstruction. The temple was declared a protected monument by the Archaeological Survey of India in 2001 and renovated by the Government of India in 2004. It is on India's UNESCO World Heritage tentative list under 'The Glorious Kakatiya Temples and Gateways' (alongside Warangal Fort and Kakatiya Kala Thoranam). In the 2020s, the ASI completed a long-running restoration of the fallen Kalyana Mandapam, rebuilding it stone-by-stone using the original Kakatiya 'sandbox' foundation technique. ASI has reportedly spent ~₹9.90 crore on restoration. The temple is NOT (and has never been) inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site — only the Ramappa Temple at Palampet (~75 km away) carries that designation (inscribed 25 July 2021, UNESCO ref 1570).

page_content:
Temple: Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple
Temple ID: T0013
Section: significance

religious_significance: The temple holds importance as a Trikutalayam housing the grouping of Shiva, Vishnu and Surya (Surya replacing Brahma in this particular grouping) within one interconnected complex — an arrangement considered relatively distinctive among South Indian temples. Trimurti Puja performed here is regarded as symbolic of unified worship of the three deities.
spiritual_significance: Devotees traditionally believe the temple's orientation was deliberately designed so that the first rays of the morning sun fall directly upon the Shiva lingam in the sanctum, reflecting the Kakatiya rulers' devotion to Shiva and their astronomical/architectural planning. The temple is popularly regarded as a symbol of the artistic and spiritual zenith of Kakatiya civilisation in Telangana.
healing_beliefs: Devotees believe the temple's serene environment and sacred vibrations promote mental peace and spiritual healing.
healing_beliefs: Pilgrimage associated with general welfare and relief from planetary afflictions through worship of the Shiva-Vishnu-Surya triad.
miracles_and_devotee_experiences: The core shrines survived 14th-century Tughlaq invasions despite damage to the Kalyana Mandapam, widely attributed to the Kakatiya 'sandbox' foundation technique (sand-filled pit absorbing seismic shocks).
miracles_and_devotee_experiences: The temple has remained standing through multiple earthquakes over the centuries, again attributed to advanced Kakatiya engineering.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple
Temple ID: T0013
Section: architecture

architecture: The temple reflects late Chalukyan and early Kakatiya architectural traditions (broadly Vesara style), built primarily of dolerite/black basalt and granite. It is a 'Trikutalayam' — a star-shaped, triple-shrine complex where the Shiva shrine faces east and the Vishnu and Surya shrines face south and west, all connected to a central mandapam so that no pillar obstructs the view of any deity. It features close to 1,000 intricately carved stone pillars, a ~6-foot monolithic Nandi carved from a single block of black basalt/dolerite facing the Shiva shrine, a restored Kalyana Mandapam (dance/marriage hall, ASI-restored in the 2020s using the original 'sandbox' foundation technique), the natya mandapam (dance hall) at the front, rock-cut elephant sculptures, perforated stone screens, finely carved doorways, and inscriptions. The structure is elevated on a 1-metre platform that slopes gently toward Hanamakonda Hill.

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: Where is the Thousand Pillar Temple located?
faq.answer: It is located at the base of Hanamakonda Hill in Hanamakonda (Hanamkonda), part of the Warangal tri-city area in Telangana, India, on the Hyderabad–Warangal Highway (NH-163), Brahmanawada. Pincode 506011.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: Who built the Thousand Pillar Temple, and when?
faq.answer: It was built in 1163 CE by the Kakatiya king Rudra Deva (Rudradeva I); construction is generally reported to have taken about 72 years (c. 1175–1324 CE build/expansion window per multiple sources).
faq.id: FAQ003
faq.question: Which deities are worshipped at the temple?
faq.answer: It is a Trikutalayam dedicated to Lord Shiva (Rudreshwara, east-facing), Lord Vishnu (south-facing) and Surya Deva (Sun God, west-facing).
faq.id: FAQ004
faq.question: What is the temple's other/official name?
faq.answer: It is officially the Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple and is locally called 'Veyyi Stambala Gudi' (Thousand Pillar Temple in Telugu).
faq.id: FAQ005
faq.question: What are the temple's visiting hours?

faq.answer: Most sources report approximately 6:00 AM to 8:00 PM daily (e.g. Tripadvisor, Inheritage, Outlook Traveller); a few sources cite 5:00 AM to 9:00 PM with extended hours during festivals. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
faq.id: FAQ006
faq.question: Is there an entry fee?
faq.answer: Most sources indicate free general entry; a few travel blogs mention a nominal fee (~₹15 Indian / ~₹200 foreign), possibly for adjoining ASI facilities. Unresolved from official sources — confirm on-site.
faq.id: FAQ007
faq.question: Who currently manages/maintains the temple?
faq.answer: It is a centrally protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), with religious administration / day-to-day worship coordinated through Telangana state authorities (Endowments Department).
faq.id: FAQ008
faq.question: Is the Thousand Pillar Temple a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.answer: No — it is on India's UNESCO tentative list (as part of 'The Glorious Kakatiya Temples and Gateways') but is not yet inscribed as a World Heritage Site. The nearby Ramappa Temple at Palampet, Mulugu district (~75 km away) was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 25 July 2021 (UNESCO reference 1570). They are two separate monuments.
faq.id: FAQ009
faq.question: Is the Thousand Pillar Temple the same as the Ramappa Temple?

metadata.location: 1000 Pillar Temple Road / Hyderabad–Warangal Highway (NH-163), Brahmanawada, near Raganna Darwaja, Hanamakonda, Telangana – 506011, India

page_content:
Temple: Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple
Temple ID: T0013
Section: faq

faq.answer: No. They are two distinct Kakatiya monuments: the Thousand Pillar Temple is in Hanamakonda, Hanamakonda District, Telangana, and is an ASI-protected monument on the UNESCO tentative list. The Ramappa Temple is in Palampet, Mulugu District, Telangana (~75 km from Hanamakonda), and is the actual UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 2021). Both share Kakatiya architectural style but differ in date (1163 CE vs 1213 CE), layout, presiding deity grouping, and protection status.
faq.id: FAQ010
faq.question: What is the best time of year to visit?
faq.answer: October to March (cooler, ~15–25°C). Maha Shivaratri (Feb/Mar) and Karthika Pournami are the most festive times but also the most crowded.
faq.id: FAQ011
faq.question: How do I reach the temple from Hyderabad?
faq.answer: By road ~150 km (~3 hours) via NH-163; by rail via Warangal Railway Station (~5–6 km) or Kazipet Junction (~7–10 km); by air via Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~150–170 km), then onward road transport.
faq.id: FAQ012
faq.question: Can people of all faiths visit?
faq.answer: Yes — multiple sources note the temple is open to visitors of all faiths, being both an active place of worship and a protected heritage/tourist site.
faq.id: FAQ013

page_content:
Temple: Sri Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy Temple, Beechupally
Temple ID: T0020
Section: overview

overview: The Sri Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy Temple (Beechupally Hanuman Temple) is one of the most cherished Hanuman shrines in Telangana, nestled along the banks of the River Krishna, on NH-44 (formerly NH-7), in Beechupally village of Itikyala Mandal, Jogulamba Gadwal district — close to the Telangana–Karnataka border. Often called Dakshina Kashi and regarded as the 'Gateway to Srisailam', it draws thousands of devotees each year — particularly Srisailam padayatris and those performing asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan) at the adjacent Pushkar Ghat. Per temple tradition, the idol was installed ~200 years ago by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya; a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' (after whom the village is named) made daily offerings, and Lord Hanuman is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'. The temple is revered as a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram where devotees seek strength, courage, freedom from fear, success in exams/jobs/court cases, and remedies for Shani and Kuja dosha. The idol, covered with a silver Kavach, is one of the few said to bear the 'Sanku Chakra' marks. A 1992-constructed Sri Rama temple stands nearby, and two islands (Gurram Gadda and Nizam Konda) dot the Krishna opposite the shrine.

The idol was installed ~200 years ago by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya; the village is named after a young tribal devotee 'Beechupally'. Temple ID: T0020
Section: history

history.section: Origin & Vijayanagara Patronage
history.content: The temple is ~200 years old (per Hyderabad Zone, xploringdestinations). Per temple tradition, the idol of Lord Hanuman was installed by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the illustrious royal guru (rajaguru) of the Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya. After installing the idol, Vyasaraya left the area. That night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and revealed that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — and so the village came to be called Beechupally, and the Lord is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'. Originally, only the Valmiki community served as priests; later, Madhwa Brahmins (with the support of the Gadwal Rulers) were also allowed to perform rituals. The Gadwal Rulers conducted the annual religious chariot festival and supported the temple; this patronage continued as a tradition. In 1950, a road bridge across the Krishna was constructed (with a later NH-7 / now NH-44 highway passing through the village), opening up trade and transit from Rayalaseema to central India. In 1992, a large Sri Rama temple was constructed a little away from the river bank, housing several other deities. The temple sits on the banks of the Krishna River, ~30 km downstream of the Jurala Hydro Electric Project, with two islands (Gurram Gadda, Nizam Konda) opposite the shrine.

religious_significance: Beechupally is a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram, popularly called Dakshina Kashi, and is regarded as the 'Gateway to Srisailam'. It is a significant stop for devotees on the way to the Srisailam Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga; many believe seeking Hanuman's blessings here before continuing to Srisailam makes the journey safer and obstacle-free. Padayatra (foot pilgrimage) groups traditionally rest and pray here, and the Pushkar Ghat is a major site for asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan) for families from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.

The deity is revered as 'Sankata Mochana Anjaneya' — the remover of troubles. The temple is sought for strength and courage, freedom from fear, success in exams/jobs/court cases, and relief from planetary doshas (particularly Shani and Kuja dosha). The deity is also believed to safeguard pilgrims during long journeys. Lockets of Sri Anjaneya are sold here and are considered powerful (per Tripadvisor visitor accounts).

architecture: The temple is built in the South Indian architectural style and is ~200 years old. The Garbhagriha (sanctum) houses a standing idol of Lord Hanuman covered with a silver Kavach, with the deity facing east and the temple facing south. Open mandapams invite the refreshing river breeze and natural light. A Siva Linga on the river bank gets wetted by the Krishna's waters during the peak monsoon. A 1992-constructed large Sri Rama temple stands a little away from the bank, with several other deities within the complex. The temple is on the banks of the Krishna River, ~30 km downstream of the Jurala Hydro Electric Project, on NH-44. The Pushkar Ghat adjacent to the temple has permanent bathing ghats built by the Telangana State government for Krishna Pushkaralu and asthi visarjan.

darshan_and_tickets.ticket_details: Sevas such as Abhishekam, Archana, Vada mala offering, and butter and sindoor seva are available at the temple counter (specific fees not published). Astikalu nimajjan (Asthi Visarjan) at the adjacent Beechupally Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust building is a one-time fee of ₹2,500 (per a single Tripadvisor reviewer, Oct 2024), and dingi (small round boat) to the river for the immersion is ₹200–300. Annadana (food) is provided by the Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust for pilgrims. Parking fee is collected at the entrance toll gate and at the river bank parking (per Tripadvisor).

travel.road: Located on NH-44 (formerly NH-7), on the Hyderabad–Kurnool highway, 200 m from the highway. ~150 km (per Tripadvisor plan41) / ~170 km (per nagesh5366) / ~200 km (per xploringdestinations) from Hyderabad. Common route: Hyderabad → Shadnagar → Kalwakurthy → Mahbubnagar → Gadwal → Beechupally. Regular TSRTC and KSRTC buses run from Hyderabad, Kurnool, Gadwal and Raichur. A road bridge constructed in 1950 across the Krishna connects the temple to the highway. The temple is 13 km from Gadwal Town.
travel.rail: Nearest railway station is Gadwal Railway Station (~13 km).
travel.air: Nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~150 km / per xploringdestinations, 4–5 hour drive).

travel_tips: Visit early morning for a peaceful darshan (especially before 8 AM, before bus and tourist traffic picks up).
travel_tips: October to March offers the best weather; monsoon is spectacular for the Krishna scenery but be prepared for slippery steps.
travel_tips: From Hyderabad, the common route runs via Shadnagar–Kalwakurthy–Mahbubnagar–Gadwal.
travel_tips: Seek Hanuman's blessings here before continuing to Srisailam, per pilgrim tradition — many devotees make this their first stop.
travel_tips: Take a holy dip at the Beechupally Pushkar Ghat during Krishna Pushkaralu; for asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan), the Brahmana Satram building is open morning to evening with a one-time fee of ₹2,500 + ₹200–300 for the dingi boat ride.
travel_tips: Temple-managed rooms (13 rooms) are free of cost on a first-come, first-served basis; for more comfort, book Haritha Hotel Gadwal (TSTDC helpline 1800-425-46464).
travel_tips: Two toll parking fees apply — at the entrance and at the river bank.

reviews.top_reviews: Tripadvisor (plan41, 'BEECHUPALLI SRI ANJANEYASWAMY TEMPLE'): 'About 150 kilometres from Hyderabad, located alongside the National Highway 44 (formerly NH 7) by the bank of the Krishna River is an ancient and strikingly beautiful temple dedicated to Lord Sri Hanuman – the faithful Helper and Devotee of Lord Sri Rama of the Raamaayana lore. He is known here as Sri Aanjaneyaswami. The place is famously known as Beechupalli. There is a Hydro-electric Power Project named Juraala located about 30 kms from this shrine. A road bridge constructed across the River Krishna in 1950 has opened up a vital connection for trade and transit from Rayalaseema region as also from Southern India to the Central India via Telangana. The shrine is located about 200 metres away from the river bank where one finds a Siva Linga that gets wetted by the river waters during the peak monsoon period. A little away from the bank was constructed in 1992 a huge temple that was dedicated to Lord Sri Raama, although one finds several other deities within this complex. The shores of Krishna River at this location are noted for: (1) carrying out obsequies to the departed souls as per the Hindu Custom and (2) performing the ceremonial bath during the 12-year-cycle period of what is known as Pushkaram. A visit to this shrine is highly recommended to those who are facing difficulties in life. The Deity here is known to be very powerful in blessing the devotees in due fulfilment of all their earthly desires.' (5/5)

reviews.top_reviews: Tripadvisor (nagesh5366, 'Hyderabad to Beechupally for Astikalu nimajjan', Oct 2024): 'Beechupally Anjaneya Swamy temple is 200 meters from the Hyd - Kurnool highway. They collect a parking fee at the entrance toll gate and there is another parking fee at river bank parking. You can drive right from the temple entrance, a small single CC road and you will see the river and the bridge. There is a building to your right which has all the arrangements for astikalu nimajjan pooja and process. They charge a one time fee of Rs. 2500 and all the things needed are provided by them. They have stools for people that can't sit on the floor. 20 minute pooja and then you step out and go to the river. Generally people taking holy dips will not like you immersing astikalu near them so the best option is to rent a dingi (small round boat) to go into the river to do the nimajjan. They charge rs. 200 to 300 for the trip. Once done do not (as per my priest), enter any temples. Just go home. The cleaners will attack you for tips. They fight, curse, etc. Temple authorities and police seem to have failed in managing these people. The place is very very dirty...steps and access to Krishna river and the entire area is unhygienic and dirty. Once you are back on the highway based on your need and timing there are a couple of decent restaurants on your way back to Hyd. I started from Manikonda around 930 am and reached around 12. 20 pm. Left at 130 pm. Back home

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: Where is Beechupally Hanuman Temple located?
faq.answer: In Beechupally (Beechupalli) village, Itikyala Mandal, Jogulamba Gadwal District, Telangana – 509125, on the banks of the River Krishna, beside NH-44 (formerly NH-7), 200 m from the highway. About 150–200 km from Hyderabad and ~30 km downstream of the Jurala Hydro Electric Project.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: Why is Beechupally Hanuman Temple famous?
faq.answer: It is renowned for its powerful idol of Lord Hanuman ('Sankata Mochana Anjaneya', remover of troubles) installed ~200 years ago by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya; the silver-Kavach-covered idol is one of the few said to bear the unique 'Sanku Chakra' marks. It is a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram, popularly called Dakshina Kashi and the 'Gateway to Srisailam', and a key stop for Srisailam padayatris and asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan) at the adjacent Pushkar Ghat.
faq.id: FAQ003
faq.question: Is Beechupally called Dakshina Kashi?

faq.answer: Yes — Beechupally is often referred to as Dakshina Kashi because of its significant spiritual value for South Indian devotees, and as the 'Gateway to Srisailam' because Srisailam padayatris traditionally halt here to seek Hanuman's blessings before continuing to the Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga.
faq.id: FAQ004
faq.question: What is the best time to visit Beechupally Hanuman Temple?
faq.answer: Monsoon (July–September) for the spectacle of the Krishna at full flow; October to March for pleasant weather; Hanuman Jayanti (April–May, Chaitra/Vaishakha) and Krishna Pushkaralu (every 12 years) are spiritually rich but crowded; Tuesdays, Saturdays and Amavasya are highly auspicious for Hanuman worship.
faq.id: FAQ005
faq.question: What are the temple timings?
faq.answer: Per Hyderabad Zone and Mindtrip: 7:00 AM–8:30 PM daily. Xploring Destinations and the user doc give 6:00 AM–8:30 PM and 5:30 AM–1:00 PM and 4:00 PM–9:00 PM (with a short afternoon break) respectively. The Astikalu nimajjan building is open separately morning to evening. Treat 7:00 AM–8:30 PM as the most authoritative single source; confirm locally.

faq.answer: Yes — many devotees believe that visiting Beechupally Hanuman Temple before heading to Srisailam is key to a safe and successful pilgrimage. Srisailam padayatris traditionally halt and pray here; the temple is also the 'Gateway to Srisailam'.
faq.id: FAQ007
faq.question: Are accommodation facilities available near the temple?
faq.answer: Yes — the Beechupally Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust manages 13 temple rooms (free of cost, first-come, first-served). Haritha Hotel Gadwal (TSTDC, ~13 km) is the closest government-tourism stay with good food and facilities; booking via TSTDC helpline 1800-425-46464. More lodging is available in Gadwal town.
faq.id: FAQ008
faq.question: Who installed the Hanuman idol?
faq.answer: Per temple tradition, Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja) — the illustrious royal guru (rajaguru) of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya — installed the idol of Lord Hanuman here ~200 years ago. After installing, Vyasaraya left; that night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and told him that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — and the village came to be called Beechupally, with the Lord locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'.

Temple: Sri Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy Temple, Beechupally
Temple ID: T0020
Section: faq

faq.answer: Astikalu nimajjan is the ancestral ash-immersion ritual performed at the Beechupally Brahmana Satram building, adjacent to the temple. A 20-minute pooja is performed with all materials provided, then the ashes are immersed in the Krishna by dingi (small round boat, ₹200–300). One-time fee of ₹2,500 per a Tripadvisor reviewer (Oct 2024) — reconfirm on-site. The building is open morning to evening. Note: per the priest's advice cited by a Tripadvisor visitor, do not enter other temples immediately after asthi visarjan.
faq.id: FAQ010
faq.question: What is special about the Hanuman idol?
faq.answer: Three unique features: (1) It is one of the few Hanuman idols said to bear the 'Sanku Chakra' (conch and discus) marks — though these are covered by the silver Kavach and not directly visible. (2) The idol is covered with a silver Kavach. (3) It is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu' after the young tribal boy who gave the village its name through his daily prayers. Lockets of Sri Anjaneya are also sold at the temple and are considered powerful.

Sri Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy Temple, Beechupally
best_time_to_visit: Monsoon (July–September) for the spectacle of the Krishna at full flow and the river bank temple scenery; October to March for pleasant weather; Hanuman Jayanti (April–May) and Krishna Pushkaralu (every 12 years) are spiritually rich but crowded; Tuesdays, Saturdays and Amavasya are highly auspicious for Hanuman worship. Avoid stepping into other temples immediately after asthi visarjan (per Tripadvisor priest's advice).

page_content:
Temple: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Dharmapuri
Temple ID: T0017
Section: overview

overview: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple (Dharmapuri Kshetram) in Dharmapuri, Jagtial District, Telangana, is one of the oldest and most revered Narasimha temples in South India. The presiding deity is Lord Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy, the man-lion incarnation (4th avatar) of Lord Vishnu, seen seated in Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) with Goddess Lakshmi — a posture considered rare. The temple sits on the southern bank of the Godavari River, which uniquely flows southward (Dakshina Vahini) here — a rare and highly auspicious geographical feature, earning Dharmapuri the epithet 'Dakshina Kashi' (Southern Varanasi) and 'Banaras of South India'. The town is also a 'Hari-Hara Kshetra' — a rare confluence of Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions, with both the Lakshmi Narasimha temple and several ancient Shiva temples in the sacred town. The complex includes the Pata (Old) Narasimha temple and the Kottha (New) Narasimha temple, reflecting cycles of destruction and reconstruction. It is one of the nine Nava Narasimha Kshetrams, has one of the largest settlements of Vedic Brahmins in Telangana, and is also called 'Teertharajamu' (king of pilgrimages). The next Godavari Pushkaralu will be hosted here in 2027.

Temple ID: T0017
Section: overview

summary: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple (Dharmapuri Kshetram) in Dharmapuri, Jagtial District, Telangana, is an ancient Narasimha shrine (built c. 850–928 AD / 1018 AD per inscriptions; rebuilt multiple times) on the southern bank of the Dakshina Vahini Godavari River, where the Godavari uniquely flows southward. One of the nine Nava Narasimha Kshetrams and a 'Hari-Hara Kshetra', it houses the rare Padmasana-form of Lakshmi Narasimha with Goddess Lakshmi, plus shrines to Ugra/Yoga/Saumya Narasimha forms, Lord Venkateswara, Lord Brahma (rare 6-ft, four-faced murti), eight Hanumans, and Lord Yama. The town has both a Pata (Old) and a Kottha (New) Narasimha temple from cycles of destruction and reconstruction (the Kottha built in 1803 AD by Panatula Narayana Deekshitulu). It is busiest during the 13-day Brahmotsavam (Phalguna Shuddha Ekadashi to Ashtami, Feb/Mar), Narasimha Jayanthi, Vaikuntha Ekadashi and the Godavari Pushkaralu (next: 2027).

history.section: Origin & Dynastic Patronage
history.content: The temple has a history spanning more than a millennium. The construction period is variously cited as 850–928 AD (Trawell) and 1018 AD (per Tripadvisor reviewer citing inscriptions); the temple was originally built by the Chalukya dynasty, with later patronage from the Rashtrakutas and the Kakatiyas. Dharmapuri has long been one of the largest settlements of Vedic Brahmins in Telangana and a centre of Vedic learning, literature, and fine arts. The town is named after King Dharma Varma, who laid the foundation of the Lord's shrine. The temple is referenced in ancient texts like the Skanda Purana and Brahmanda Purana as 'Dharmapura', and is linked to legends of Lord Narasimha's meditation after slaying the demon Hiranyakashipu to protect his devotee Prahlada. It is also believed that Lord Rama visited this site and installed a sacred linga here.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Dharmapuri
Temple ID: T0017
Section: history

history.content: The temple was demolished by Muslim rulers during 1422–1436 AD (Rustumdil Khan, the Subedar of Hyderabad, with the support of Aurangzeb, is said to have converted it to a mosque), and was rebuilt in the 17th century, regaining its status as a major Vaishnava shrine. The Kottha (New) Narasimha Swamy Temple, also known as Sri Ugra Narasimha Swamy Temple, was built in 1803 AD by Panatula Narayana Deekshitulu and stands to the right of the Pata Narasimha temple. The temple is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department (one of 19 major temples with annual income above ₹1 crore, per the 2015 Trust Board notification). For the 2027 Godavari Pushkaralu, the Telangana government has allocated ₹50 crore for renovation, including ₹80 lakh for a new toilet complex and ₹3.1 crore for four VIP suites. The temple is a major centre for Vedic Brahmin scholars in Telangana and one of the nine Nava Narasimha Kshetrams.

religious_significance: Dharmapuri is regarded as one of the holiest Narasimha temples in South India and one of the Nava Narasimha Kshetrams (nine major Narasimha shrines). It is a rare 'Hari-Hara Kshetra' — a confluence of Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions, with both the Lakshmi Narasimha temple and several ancient Shiva temples in the sacred town. It is also called 'Dakshina Kashi' (Southern Varanasi) and 'Teertharajamu' (king of pilgrimages). Lord Narasimha is worshipped here as the protector of righteousness and the destroyer of evil. The presiding deity in Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) is considered a rare form.
spiritual_significance: Devotees believe sincere prayers remove fear, protect families, and bring peace, prosperity and spiritual growth. The temple houses multiple forms of Lord Narasimha — peaceful and fierce manifestations (Yoga, Ugra, Saumya). The Dakshina Vahini Godavari holy bath is central to its spiritual practice, believed to purify body and soul. The temple is especially sought for protection, courage, prosperity, relief from difficulties, and for child-related and family blessings. Devotees also perform Gho Pooja for wealth and for removal of enemies.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Dharmapuri
Temple ID: T0017
Section: architecture

architecture: The temple reflects a Dravidian style with towering gopurams, intricate carvings depicting scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, and spacious mandapams including the Mukha, Garuda and Kalyana halls, leading to the sanctum via the Simha Dwaram (Lion Gate). The main deity is in a serene Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) pose flanked by Goddess Lakshmi. The complex includes three forms of Narasimha — Yoga, Ugra and Saumya — and rare sub-shrines: an idol of Yama (Dharmaraju) at the entrance, eight Hanuman murtis, and a unique 6-foot, four-faced Brahma murti (one of the few in South India). Smaller shrines house Lord Venkateswara, Sri Venugopala Swamy, Sri Prasannanjaneya Swamy, Sri Ramalingeshwara Swamy, and a Pushkarini (temple tank). The Pata (Old) and Kottha (New) Narasimha temples stand side by side. Per dharmapurikshetram.in, the temple is being prepared for the 2027 Pushkaralu with new toilet complexes and VIP suites.

festivals.description: The most significant annual festival — a 13-day celebration held from Phalguna Shuddha Ekadashi to Phalguna Shuddha Ashtami (Feb/Mar). 2025: 10–22 March (per Deccan Chronicle). 2026: 27 February – 11 March (per sanatanavibes). Highlights include Ankurarpana, the divine wedding (Kalyanotsavam) of Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy and Sri Venkateswara Swamy, Teppotsavam (float festival on the Godavari), Dolotsavam of Sri Yoga Narasimha Swamy, the Muvvur Swamulu chariot procession, and grand processions. Guided spiritually by Paramahamsa Parivrājaka Āchārya (head of Dharmapuri Mutt) and Sri Sri Sri Satchidananda Saraswati Maharaj.

Men generally wear dhoti, kurta or formal Indian clothing; women are encouraged to wear sarees, salwar kameez or other traditional dresses. Shorts, sleeveless clothing and revealing outfits are discouraged. Footwear must be removed before entering, silence should be maintained in the sanctum, and photography may be restricted near the main deity.

The sacred town also has choultries. Nearby towns Jagtial (~30 km), Mancherial (~40 km), Karimnagar (~70–75 km) and Ramagundam (~65 km) offer more options, including premium accommodation.

accommodation.price_range: Temple guest rooms ~₹300–₹800 per day (family/special rooms higher). Private hotels and lodges in Dharmapuri ~₹800–₹2,500 per night.

reviews.top_reviews: Tripadvisor (Suryakatakam, 'One of the Nava Narasimha Kshetram'): 'Dharmapuri Temple is one of the Nava Narasimha kshetram, which is located @30 km away from district headquarter of Jagityala. Nearest Railway station is Manchiryala Railway station which is @40 km away from this temple. History of Temple: This temple is built on the banks of Godavari District. was built in 1018 AD as per the inscriptions. This temple was demolished by the Muslim rulers in 1422-1436 AD and Rebuilt in 17th Century. The foundation of the Lord Shrine was layed by the king of the area. The name of the king was Dharma Varma and the town derived its name as Dharmapuri from the name of the king. This town is also known as "Dakshina Kashi" and also called as Banaras of South India. This temple will be crowded heavily on Nrusimha Jayanthi, Vaikunat Ekadashi and Karthika Pournami Celebrations. We Visited this temple as one day trip from Hyderabad. Temple Timings: Morning 05:00-02:00, Evening 04:00-08:00.' (5/5)

reviews.top_reviews: Deccan Chronicle 9 March 2025 (Puli Sharath Kumar): 'The district administration, in collaboration with the endowment department, has made extensive preparations for the prestigious Brahmotsavam (Jatara) celebrations of Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy and Sri Venkateswara Swamy at Dharmapuri in Jagtial district. The 13-day festival will start on March 10, coinciding with the auspicious Phalguna Shuddha Ekadashi, and conclude on March 22. Located on the sacred banks of the Godavari River, the event will be marked by grandeur and devotion. The festivities will be guided spiritually by Paramahamsa Parivrājaka Āchārya, head of Dharmapuri Mutt, and Sri Sri Sri Satchidananda Saraswati Maharaj. Highlights include the divine wedding of Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy and Sri Venkateswara Swamy on March 11, followed by a ritual float procession (Teppotsavam) and Dolotsavam of Sri Yoga Narasimha Swamy on March 14.'

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: Where is Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple located?
faq.answer: The temple is located in Dharmapuri, Dharmapuri Mandal, Jagtial District, Telangana, on the southern bank of the Godavari River (Dakshina Vahini). Pincode 505425. About 220–245 km from Hyderabad; ~30 km from Jagtial; ~40 km from Mancherial Railway Station.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: Which deity is worshipped in the temple?
faq.answer: The presiding deity is Lord Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy (the 4th incarnation of Lord Vishnu) in the rare Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) form, accompanied by Goddess Lakshmi. The complex also includes three forms of Narasimha (Yoga, Ugra, Saumya), Lord Venkateswara, eight Hanuman murtis, a rare 6-ft four-faced Brahma murti, Lord Yama at the entrance, and Lord Shiva shrines (Hari-Hara Kshetra).

Temple ID: T0017
Section: faq

faq.answer: It is famous for being one of the nine Nava Narasimha Kshetrams, for its location on the sacred Dakshina Vahini (southward-flowing) Godavari River, for being called 'Dakshina Kashi' (Southern Varanasi) and 'Teertharajamu' (king of pilgrimages), for the rare Padmasana-form of Lord Lakshmi Narasimha, and for its status as a Hari-Hara Kshetra (Vaishnava-Shaiva harmony). The town has one of the largest settlements of Vedic Brahmins in Telangana. The next Godavari Pushkaralu is 26 June – 7 July 2027.
faq.id: FAQ004
faq.question: What are the temple timings?
faq.answer: Per the JustDial official listing and dharmapurikshetram.in: 5:30 AM–2:30 PM and 4:00 PM–8:00 PM daily. The temple opens with Suprabhata Seva at 5:00 AM. Some other sources (Tripadvisor, Trawell, Grokipedia) give 5:00 AM–2:00 PM and 4:00 PM–8:00 PM. The 2:30 PM–4:00 PM break for darshanam is confirmed. Hours are extended during the 13-day Brahmotsavam, Narasimha Jayanthi, Vaikuntha Ekadashi and Godavari Pushkaralu.

faq.question: Is there an entry fee for darshan?

faq.answer: No. General darshan is free for all devotees. Special sevas require paid tickets: Abhishekam ₹150, Nitya Kalyanam ₹500, Sudarshana Homam ₹316, Kumkumarchana ₹100, Marriage ₹2,116, Upanayanam ₹1,516, Ganda Deepam ₹5, Swamy Aarti ₹10, plus Saswatha (perpetual) endowment poojas ranging from ₹1,116 to ₹25,116.
faq.id: FAQ006
faq.question: Which is the biggest festival celebrated here?
faq.answer: The 13-day Brahmotsavam (Phalguna Shuddha Ekadashi to Phalguna Shuddha Ashtami, Feb/Mar) is the most significant — with Kalyanotsavam, Teppotsavam (float festival on the Godavari), Dolotsavam of Sri Yoga Narasimha Swamy, and the Muvvur Swamulu chariot procession. The 2025 Brahmotsavam was 10–22 March; the 2026 one is 27 February – 11 March. Narasimha Jayanthi, Vaikuntha Ekadashi and the Godavari Pushkaralu (next: 2027) are also major celebrations.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Dharmapuri
Temple ID: T0017
Section: faq

faq.answer: The Godavari River, which generally flows west to east, uniquely flows from north to south (Dakshina Vahini) at Dharmapuri — a rare and highly auspicious geographical feature. Pilgrims traditionally take a holy dip in this stretch of the Godavari before entering the temple, believing it purifies body and soul. The site is called 'Dakshina Kashi' (Southern Varanasi) because of this feature. The next Godavari Pushkaralu at this site is 26 June – 7 July 2027.
faq.id: FAQ010
faq.question: What is special about the Padmasana-form of Lord Lakshmi Narasimha here?
faq.answer: Unlike the usual fierce, standing form of Lord Narasimha, the presiding deity at Dharmapuri is seen seated in Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) with his palms bending on his knees, accompanied by Goddess Lakshmi. Such a yogic posture is considered a rare form of the Lord and is one of the temple's defining features. The main deity is flanked by three forms of Narasimha — Yoga, Ugra and Saumya — symbolising peaceful, fierce and gentle aspects of the Lord.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Bhadrakali Temple
Temple ID: T0012
Section: overview

overview: Sri Bhadrakali Temple is one of the oldest and most revered temples dedicated to Goddess Bhadrakali in India. Located between Warangal and Hanamkonda in Telangana, it stands on the banks of the picturesque Bhadrakali Lake, surrounded by rocky hills and lush greenery. The temple is dedicated to Goddess Bhadrakali, a powerful form of Goddess Parvati symbolising courage, protection, prosperity and divine energy. The presiding deity is a magnificent single-stone (Ekashila) idol nearly 2.7 metres tall, depicted with eight arms holding divine weapons and a fierce expression. Originally built during the Chalukya dynasty (traditionally dated 625 AD by Pulakeshin II after his Vengi victory) and later patronised by the Kakatiyas — who worshipped her as their Kula Devatha (family deity) and built the adjoining Bhadrakali Lake — it is one of the most vibrant Shakti temples in South India, especially during Vasanta Navaratri, Sharannavaratri, Bonalu and Bathukamma. Stone and Goddess statues also dot the surrounding hills, making the entire hilltop a sacred landscape.

summary: Sri Bhadrakali Temple in Tadkamalla Village (Hanamkonda/Warangal), Telangana, is an ancient Shakti temple on the banks of Bhadrakali Lake, dedicated to Goddess Bhadrakali (a fierce form of Parvati). Built in 625 AD (traditionally by Chalukya King Pulakeshin II after his Vengi victory) and later patronised by the Kakatiyas as their Kula Devatha, it is famed for its ~2.7-metre Ekashila (single-stone) eight-armed idol. Regarded as one of the most sacred Shakti Peethas in Telangana, it draws lakhs of devotees during Vasanta Navaratri, Sharannavaratri, Bonalu and Bathukamma. Architecture blends Chalukyan and Kakatiya styles; surrounding hills have additional God/Goddess statues.

history.section: Origin (Chalukya Era, 625 AD)
history.content: The temple has a history dating back to 625 AD and is believed to have been constructed by Chalukya King Pulakeshin II after his victory over the Vengi region. The king dedicated the temple to Goddess Bhadrakali as an expression of gratitude for her divine blessings and protection during his military campaign. It is one of the earliest examples of Chalukyan temple architecture in Telangana.
history.foundation_year: 625 AD (traditional)
history.founders: Chalukya King Pulakeshin II (traditionally attributed)
history.legends: Pulakeshin II built the temple as gratitude to Goddess Bhadrakali after his Vengi victory.
history.legends: The temple is one of the earliest Chalukyan-era stone temples in the Telangana region.
history.section: Kakatiya Patronage & Revival (12th–14th century CE)
history.content: During the Kakatiya dynasty the temple gained even greater prominence. The Kakatiya rulers — including Rudrama Devi — regarded Goddess Bhadrakali as their family deity (Kula Devatha) and contributed significantly to the temple's development; they also constructed the nearby Bhadrakali Lake, which served as an important water reservoir. The temple reflects a blend of Chalukyan and Kakatiya architectural styles. After the fall of the Kakatiya Empire, the temple gradually lost prominence but was revived in the mid-20th century through restoration efforts led by devotees and temple authorities.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Bhadrakali Temple
Temple ID: T0012
Section: significance

religious_significance: Sri Bhadrakali Temple is regarded as one of the most sacred Shakti Peethas in Telangana. Devotees worship Goddess Bhadrakali as the embodiment of Shakti (divine feminine energy), believing she protects from evil, removes obstacles, and blesses with courage, prosperity and peace. As the Kula Devatha of the Kakatiya rulers, it holds immense historical and spiritual significance. The temple is especially popular among students, newly married couples, business owners and families seeking success and protection.
spiritual_significance: The 2.7-metre Ekashila idol represents both fierce power and compassionate motherhood. Devotees believe offerings of kumkum, coconuts, sarees, bangles, turmeric and special prayers fulfil sincere wishes. The serene Bhadrakali Lake setting — with sun reflecting off the water onto the temple during early morning and evening — enhances worship and meditation. The temple is also a major centre for Chandi Homam and Sri Chakra Pooja for those seeking protection and prosperity.
healing_beliefs: Protection from evil, black magic and negative influences
healing_beliefs: Removal of obstacles; blessings for success in education, career, business and competitive exams

page_content:
Temple: Sri Bhadrakali Temple
Temple ID: T0012
Section: architecture

architecture: The temple showcases a beautiful blend of Chalukyan and Kakatiya architectural styles. Situated on a rocky hillock overlooking Bhadrakali Lake, it preserves several ancient stone pillars and structural elements near the sanctum despite renovations over the years. The main attraction is the magnificent Ekashila (single-stone) idol of Goddess Bhadrakali, about 2.7 metres tall, in a seated posture with eight arms holding divine weapons. The complex houses shrines to Lord Shiva, Lord Ganesha and other deities. Surrounding hills feature statues of various Gods and Goddesses; the entire setting amid gardens, the lake and rocky landscape is considered a sacred Shakti Kshetra.
architectural_style: Blend of Chalukyan (7th century CE) and Kakatiya (12th–14th century CE) architecture

dress_code: Devotees are encouraged to wear traditional and modest clothing. Men generally wear dhoti, kurta or formal Indian attire; women are advised to wear sarees, salwar kameez or other decent traditional dresses. Shorts, sleeveless clothing and revealing outfits are discouraged. Footwear must be removed before entering, silence should be maintained in the sanctum, and photography may be restricted in certain areas. Telangana Tourism advises carrying water, light snacks, hats or umbrellas in summer.

travel.road: Approximately 150 km from Hyderabad, 3–4 hours via National Highway 163. TGSRTC operates frequent buses from Hyderabad, Karimnagar, Khammam, Nizamabad, Adilabad, Nalgonda and Siddipet; APSRTC connects from Vijayawada, Guntur, Visakhapatnam and Rajahmundry. Special buses run during Bonalu, Navaratri and Brahmotsavam. The temple is in the heart of the city and is easily reachable by auto-rickshaw at minimal cost.
travel.rail: Nearest station is Warangal Railway Station (~2–5 km), a major junction on the Delhi–Chennai main line, connected to Hyderabad, Vijayawada, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Bengaluru, Nagpur, Delhi and Mumbai. Kazipet Junction (~10 km) is another option. Auto-rickshaws, taxis and city buses are available from both stations.
travel.air: Nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~160–170 km). Reach Warangal by taxi, TGSRTC airport bus, train or private vehicle. Warangal Airport is also operational for limited regional connectivity (per Wikipedia infobox).

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: Where is Sri Bhadrakali Temple located?
faq.answer: The temple is located in Tadkamalla Village, Hanamkonda, Warangal, Telangana – 506007, on the banks of Bhadrakali Lake between Warangal and Hanamkonda.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: Which deity is worshipped in the temple?
faq.answer: The temple is dedicated to Goddess Bhadrakali, a powerful (fierce) form of Goddess Parvati. The presiding deity is a ~2.7-metre Ekashila (single-stone) eight-armed idol.
faq.id: FAQ003
faq.question: What is Bhadrakali Temple famous for?
faq.answer: It is famous for its 2.7-metre-tall Ekashila (single-stone) idol of Goddess Bhadrakali, the stunning lakeside setting, and its historical association with the Kakatiya dynasty, who worshipped her as their Kula Devatha. The temple is dated to 625 AD (Chalukyan era).

faq.answer: The temple is open daily from 5:30 AM to 1:00 PM and 3:00 PM to 8:30 PM. Alankara Darshan 6:00–7:30 AM, Sarva Darshan 7:30 AM–12:00 PM, Maha Mangala Aarti 12:00–12:30 PM, Sarva Darshan 3:00–7:00 PM, Special Darshan 7:00–8:00 PM, Ekantha Seva 8:00–8:30 PM. Hours are extended during festivals.
faq.id: FAQ005
faq.question: Is there an entry fee for darshan?
faq.answer: No — general (Sarva) darshan is free. Paid options: Alankara Darshan ₹100, Maha Mangala Aarti ₹200, Special Darshan ₹500, Ekantha Seva ₹100. Seva tickets at the temple counter.
faq.id: FAQ006
faq.question: Which is the biggest festival celebrated here?
faq.answer: Sharannavaratri and Vasanta Navaratri are the grandest festivals (nine days each), followed by Bonalu, Bathukamma, Bhadrakali Brahmotsavam, Shakambari Utsavam, Durga Ashtami, Ugadi, Maha Shivaratri, Karthika Masam and Deepavali.

faq.question: Is accommodation available near the temple?

faq.answer: Yes. Numerous hotels, lodges and guest houses are available in Hanamkonda and Warangal (the temple itself has limited on-campus accommodation). Haritha Hotel (Telangana Tourism), Hotel Suprabha, City Inn, Shreemaya and Ratna are popular options.
faq.id: FAQ008
faq.question: What is the best time to visit Bhadrakali Temple?
faq.answer: October to February for pleasant weather; early morning (6:00–8:00 AM) or evening (5:00–7:00 PM) for beautiful lake reflections. For a grand experience, visit during Sharannavaratri, Vasanta Navaratri, Bonalu or Bathukamma (very crowded).
faq.id: FAQ009
faq.question: Who built the Bhadrakali Temple?
faq.answer: Traditionally built in 625 AD by Chalukya King Pulakeshin II as a votive offering after his Vengi victory. The Kakatiya dynasty (12th–14th c. CE) later worshipped Goddess Bhadrakali as their Kula Devatha and built the adjoining Bhadrakali Lake.
faq.id: FAQ010
faq.question: What is the Ekashila idol?
faq.answer: The Ekashila (single-stone) idol of Goddess Bhadrakali is approximately 2.7 metres tall, depicted in a seated posture with eight arms holding divine weapons and a fierce expression. It is one of the largest single-stone Devi idols in Telangana and a major draw for devotees.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Temple, Komuravelli
Temple ID: T0015
Section: overview

overview: The Komuravelli Mallanna Temple (Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Devasthanam) is one of the most powerful and culturally vibrant folk-deity temples in Telangana. Located on a low hill (Indrakeeladri) in Komuravelli village, Cherial Mandal, Siddipet district, about 85–95 km from Hyderabad on SH-1 Rajiv Rahadari (Karimnagar–Hyderabad Highway), it is devoted to Lord Mallanna (Mallikarjuna Swamy) — a fierce yet compassionate folk incarnation of Lord Shiva (in 'vigraha rupam' / murti form, with consorts Golla Kethamma and Medalamma), also venerated as Khandoba by Maharashtrian devotees. Unlike traditional Agama-based temples, it embodies Telangana's living folk traditions where devotion is expressed through the Oggu Katha narrative tradition, folk offerings, and vows rather than formal Vedic sevas. The 8-foot clay idol is believed to be ~500 years old. The temple is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department (Dy. Commissioner & Executive Officer). Its signature event is the Komuravelli Mallanna Jathara, one of the biggest folk festivals in Telangana.

summary: The Komuravelli Mallanna Temple (Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Temple) at Komuravelli, Cherial Mandal, Siddipet district, Telangana, is a major folk-deity shrine dedicated to Lord Mallanna — a Telangana folk form of Lord Shiva (also worshipped as Khandoba) — with consorts Golla Kethamma and Medalamma. Set on Indrakeeladri hill ~85–95 km from Hyderabad, it is rooted in oral tradition and the Oggu Katha folk-narrative form (in Telugu, not Sanskrit) rather than Agama ritual. Worshipped as a guardian deity (Grama Devata) who delivers swift justice and protection, it draws lakhs during the annual Mallanna Jathara (every Sunday from Makara Sankranti to Ugadi) and large crowds every Sunday and Monday. The temple is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department under the Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Devasthanam Board.

Section: history

history.section: Origins & Folk Tradition
history.content: The temple's history stretches back several centuries and is rooted in oral tradition rather than written records. According to popular tradition, Komaranna, a devotee from the Yadava community, performed deep penance (tapas) for Lord Shiva on this hilltop. Lord Shiva appeared before him as Mallanna, and Komaranna installed the divine 8-foot clay idol on the hill, establishing the shrine. A separate popular legend holds that Lord Mallikarjuna appeared in a dream to a shepherd and told him he was enshrined on Indrakeeladri hill in 'Putta Matti' (soft earth) to fulfill devotees' desires. The current clay idol is believed to be ~500 years old. Worship of Mallanna originally flourished among shepherds, farmers and warriors, and over time the site transformed into a major pilgrimage centre attracting devotees from across Telangana. As the rush of devotees increased, the temple committee (and later the Endowments Department) renovated the temple complex, built mandapams, choultries, rest rooms, water facilities, and the 200+ room accommodation block. The Mallanna story has no written script — it is preserved and sung in the Oggu Katha folk-narrative tradition by the Oggu community.

sthala_puranam: Lord Mallanna, the Telangana folk-form of Lord Shiva, is revered as a guardian deity (Grama Devata) of villages, livestock and the rural poor. According to popular tradition, Komaranna of the Yadava community performed intense penance on Indrakeeladri hill, and Lord Shiva appeared before him as Mallanna. Komaranna installed the 8-foot clay idol, which remains the presiding deity. Mallanna's story — unwritten and transmitted orally — is performed in the Oggu Katha by hereditary singer-storytellers (the Oggu community), who narrate his exploits and his marriage to the goddess Medalamma after overcoming the conditions set by her brothers. Devotees believe Mallanna hears prayers directly and delivers immediate justice, mediating land, legal and family conflicts.

Section: significance

religious_significance: Mallanna is at the heart of Telangana's folk devotion, embodying faith, social justice and community bonding that bridges castes and classes. He is seen as a champion of justice and truth, a mediator for land, legal and family conflicts, a protector of villages and livestock, and a vanquisher of fear, evil spirits and negative energies. Devotees regard him as a 'living god' who hears prayers directly without intermediaries. He is especially popular among the Kuruma, Mudhiraj, Yadava and other BC communities. The temple is one of the prominent Shiva shrines in northern Telangana, alongside Vemulawada (Rajarajeshwara) and Kaleshwaram (Mukteshwara).
spiritual_significance: The temple is believed to be a sacred spot for instant justice and divine protection. Devotees come seeking help with health issues, court cases, family concerns and land disputes. Unlike classical Agama temples, worship here is heartfelt, emotional and woven into everyday rural life, expressed through folk offerings and vows rather than formal paid rituals. All mantras are chanted in Telugu (not Sanskrit) — a distinctive inclusive tradition that sets this temple apart from most major Indian shrines.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Temple, Komuravelli
Temple ID: T0015
Section: architecture

architecture: The temple is built in a simple folk-temple style (no towering gopurams) and is located in a cave on the Indrakeeladri hillock, reached by a short climb of about 100 steps. The main sanctum houses Lord Mallanna in a humble folk style as a seated 8-foot clay murti in 'vigraha rupam' (statue form) rather than the more common 'linga rupam'. The complex includes a Medalamma (consort) sannidhi, subsidiary shrines for Ganesha, Nandi and the Navagrahas (on an elevated platform), and a Veera Bhadra cave temple (with a sacred Shiva Linga and Nandi) reached by climbing a few more steps. There are separate passages for entrance and exit from the cave temple. The main entrance tower, compound wall, Mukhamantapa and cottages are painted in yellow to mark them as temple property. The complex has a spacious open courtyard for large gatherings, and ~200 rooms for devotees' accommodation managed by the Devasthanam Board.

The most-detailed sources (xploringdestinations.com, templemama.com, multiple Tripadvisor reviews citing the in-situ board) consistently give: temple open 4:30 AM–8:30 PM, with a fixed 12:00 PM–3:00 PM afternoon closure, and general darshan 6:00 AM–12:00 PM and 3:00 PM–7:00 PM. Grokipedia gives 4:00 AM–9:00 PM; a minority of blogs cite 5:00 AM–10:00 PM (extended to near-24x7 during Jathara). The internal ritual schedule (Oggu Prathana, Suprabhatam, Theertha Binde, Darshanam, Nivedana) is also documented. Confirm locally before visiting. Other resolved conflicts: mandal is Cherial Mandal (per official EO address); the Wikipedia text placing it in 'Warangal District' is pre-2022 (Siddipet District is the correct current district).

festivals.description: The temple's signature annual observance — one of the biggest folk festivals in Telangana. Runs every Sunday from Makara Sankranti (mid-January) to Ugadi (March–April), about 10 Sundays. Largest crowds (50,000–100,000) on the first Sunday after Sankranti and the final Sunday before Ugadi.

reviews.top_reviews: A very beautiful experience in scenic surroundings (Tripadvisor, Dec 2021): 'Navagrahas are seen on an elevated platform. If one climbs a few steps further, there is a cave temple for Veera Bhadra along with an idol of a sacred Shiva Linga and Nandi. There is a temple for Konda Pochamma at a distance of 20 kms from this place. Devotees worship Konda Pochamma and offer bonams on Tuesday. In Mallanna's temple, turmeric powder called Bandari is applied on the brows of devotees. The main entrance tower, the compound wall, Mukhamantapa and cottages are painted in yellow. There are separate passages for entrance and exit from the cave temple. Devotees can avail quick darshan by paying one hundred rupees each. Devotees buy Bandari packets from pooja stall as they believe that bandari protects devotees from all diseases. Outside the temple there are many stalls selling pooja materials. The Endowments Department renovated the temple mantapams and choultries. Nearly two hundred rooms are made available for devotees' accommodation by Komuravelli Devasthanam Board. The temple is open from 4.30 a.m. to 8.30 p.m. and from 12.00 p.m. to 3.00 p.m. The darshan timings are from 6.00 a.m. to 12.00 p.m. and from 3.00 p.m. to 7.00 p.m. Scenic surroundings, the idols in the cave and the hillock with beautiful sculptures.'

faq.id: FAQ001
faq.question: Where can I find Komuravelli Mallanna Temple?
faq.answer: Komuravelli Mallanna Temple is in Komuravelli village, Cherial Mandal, Siddipet district, Telangana, roughly 85–95 km from Hyderabad on SH-1 Rajiv Rahadari. Pincode 506 223.
faq.id: FAQ002
faq.question: Who do people worship at Komuravelli Temple?
faq.answer: The temple is dedicated to Lord Mallanna (Mallikarjuna Swamy), a revered folk representation of Lord Shiva appearing in 'vigraha rupam' (murti) form, with consorts Golla Kethamma (Yadava community) and Medalamma / Bramarambika (Linga Balija community). He is also venerated as Khandoba by Maharashtrian devotees.
faq.id: FAQ003
faq.question: What makes Komuravelli Mallanna Temple spiritually significant?
faq.answer: It is considered a sacred spot for instant justice and divine protection, where devotees seek help with health issues, legal matters, family concerns and land disputes. All mantras are chanted in Telugu (not Sanskrit), and the Oggu Katha folk-narrative tradition preserves Mallanna's story.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Temple, Komuravelli
Temple ID: T0015
Section: faq

faq.answer: The temple does not follow formal Agama-based rituals. Devotees make folk offerings — breaking coconuts, bonam, kode mokku (bull offering) and patnam rangoli. The daily internal ritual schedule is: Oggu Prathana 4:00–4:30 AM; Suprabhatam Seva 4:30–5:00 AM; Theertha Binde & Rudrabhishekam 5:00–6:00 AM and 7:15 PM; Darshanam 6:00 AM–12:00 PM and 3:00–7:00 PM; Maha Nivedana 12:00 PM; Nivedana 8:00 PM. Reserved sevas, special poojas and annadanam are available online via the Devasthanam Board.
faq.id: FAQ007
faq.question: When is the best time to visit Komuravelli Mallanna Temple?
faq.answer: Mondays, Sundays, Amavasya days and the Sankranti-to-Ugadi Jathara season are the most auspicious times. A mid-Jathara Sunday offers a vibrant atmosphere with smaller crowds. Early weekday mornings are best for peaceful, crowd-free darshan.

faq.answer: Take a TSRTC bus from JBS/MGBS to Siddipet or Gajwel (~₹100–200 one-way), then a local bus, auto or shared jeep to Komuravelli village. Special buses run on Mondays, Sundays and during the Jathara. By road it is ~85–95 km (~2–2.5 hours) on SH-1 Rajiv Rahadari.
faq.id: FAQ009
faq.question: Is there any accommodation near Komuravelli Temple?
faq.answer: Yes — the Komuravelli Devasthanam Board provides ~200+ rooms on the temple premises, painted yellow to mark them as registered temple property. Rooms are first-come, first-served (no online advance booking) and fill quickly on Mondays, Sundays and during the Jathara. Most devotees otherwise prefer staying in nearby Gajwel or Siddipet.
faq.id: FAQ010
faq.question: What is Komuravelli Jathara?
faq.answer: Komuravelli Jathara is a grand annual folk festival running every Sunday from Makara Sankranti (mid-January) to Ugadi (March–April), drawing lakhs of devotees with bull offerings (kode mokku), vow fulfillment, Oggu Katha performances, fire observances (Agni Gundaalu) and cultural events. The 'Pedda Patnam' on Maha Shivaratri also draws lakhs of pilgrims.

page_content:
Temple: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Jamalapuram
Temple ID: T0018
Section: overview

overview: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple at Jamalapuram, in Yerrupalem Mandal of Khammam District, Telangana, is popularly known as 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati', 'Khammam Chinna Tirupati' or 'Telangana Tirupati', reflecting devotees' belief that the deity here is comparably powerful and auspicious to Lord Venkateswara at Tirumala. The presiding deity is a self-manifested (Swayambhu) form of Lord Vishnu, worshipped as 'Balaji' in stone (vigraha) form with consorts Sri Padmavathi and Sri Alamelu (Alivelu) Ammavaru. Recognised as a Swayam Vyakta kshetra (per the official Telangana Tourism portal), it is one of the older Vaishnavite shrines in Khammam district — believed to be over 800–850 years old per the main priest (Uppala Srinivasa Sarma) and 'over 1,000 years old' per tourism sources. It was visited by the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra on his way to Tiruvuru and renovated in the early 16th century by Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya en route to Kondapalli fort during his 'Jaitra Yatra'. A statue of Sri Krishnadevaraya stands near the Pongali Mandapam (installed c. 2010 to mark the 500th anniversary of his coronation). The temple draws large crowds, especially on Saturdays and during Brahmotsavam, Vaikunta Ekadasi and Dwadasi.

summary: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple at Jamalapuram (Yerrupalem Mandal, Khammam district, Telangana) is a Vaishnavite shrine to a Swayambhu Venkateswara ('Balaji') with consorts Padmavathi and Alamelu, popularly called 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati'. Believed to be 800–1,000+ years old (per the main priest and tourism sources), it was visited by the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra and renovated by Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya in the early 16th century. Two founding legends link it to sage Jabali's penance at Suchi Gutta (Soochi Giri) and to the devotee Uppala Yagnanarayana Sharma / his descendant Uppala Akku Bhatlu, after whom the deity is said to have self-manifested.
